lessons.title: Complex powers, rotations and root arguments
lessons.summary: Connect algebra, modulus and the angle of a complex number.
lessons.objective: Use de Moivre’s theorem for integer powers and list every root with the requested argument convention.
lessons.before: Review complex arithmetic, conjugates, the Argand diagram and the sine/cosine addition formulae. The modulus of a+bi is the non-negative square root of \(a^{2}\)+\(b^{2}\); an argument is an angle modulo 2π. Review induction before the proof.
lessons.ideas:
Keep modulus and argument separate

\[\begin{gathered}z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)=re^{i\theta},\qquad r>0\\z^n=r^ne^{in\theta}\quad(n\in\mathbb Z)\end{gathered}\]

The zero complex number has modulus zero but no argument. A negative integer power needs a non-zero base. Multiplying non-zero complex numbers multiplies their moduli and adds their arguments modulo 2π; division divides the moduli and subtracts the arguments.

Why the integer-power rule holds

For n=1 the statement is the original polar representation. Suppose it holds for n=k. Multiplication by the original number, followed by the angle-addition formulae, gives the representation with modulus \(r^{k+1}\) and angle (k+1)θ. This proves the positive integer cases by induction. The zero power is 1. Taking reciprocals gives the negative cases, with reciprocal modulus and reversed angle.

Multiplication is a rotation and a scaling

The map w=λz, with non-zero λ, rotates about the origin through arg λ and scales distances by |λ|. A negative argument represents a clockwise rotation; adding a full turn describes the same map. Translation is a separate operation and changes the centre of a root polygon.

An equation has all of its roots

\[\begin{gathered}z^m=Re^{i\phi}\quad(R>0)\\z_k=R^{1/m}e^{i(\phi+2k\pi)/m}\\k=0,1,\ldots,m-1\end{gathered}\]

These are m distinct roots, equally spaced on a circle. Taking only the principal mth root misses the others. Find them all first, then reduce each argument to the requested half-open interval. For a negative-power equation, first rewrite it as a positive-power equation without allowing zero.
lessons.method:
1. Write the non-zero base in modulus–argument form.
  2. Multiply or divide the argument and transform the modulus as required.
  3. For a root equation include every 2kπ branch before division.
  4. Reduce angles into the stated interval without duplicating an endpoint.
  5. Check the original equation and describe any rotation about the correct centre.
mistakes: A negative exponent inverts the modulus as well as the angle.
Zero has no argument and cannot be raised to a negative power.
There are m roots of a non-zero mth-power equation, not one.
The two endpoints of a full-turn argument interval represent the same direction.
Arguments after a translation describe displacement from the centre, not from the origin.

examples.title: 1 · An exact fifth power
examples.question: Evaluate \((\sqrt3+i)^5\) in Cartesian form.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sqrt3+i=2e^{i\pi/6}\\(\sqrt3+i)^5=32e^{5i\pi/6}\\=-16\sqrt3+16i\end{gathered}\]

The modulus is raised to the fifth power. The angle is multiplied by five, rather than exponentiated.

examples.title: 2 · A negative power
examples.question: Evaluate \((1-i)^{-3}\) exactly.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}1-i=\sqrt2e^{-i\pi/4}\\(1-i)^{-3}=\frac1{2\sqrt2}e^{3i\pi/4}\\=-\frac14+\frac14i\end{gathered}\]

Multiplying this result by (1−i)³ gives 1, providing an algebraic check.

examples.title: 3 · Describe the complete transformation
examples.question: Let \(w=\frac{-1+i\sqrt3}{4}z\). Describe the map and find the image of z=4.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\lambda=\frac12e^{2i\pi/3}\\|\lambda|=\frac12,\qquad\arg\lambda=\frac{2\pi}{3}\\w(4)=-1+i\sqrt3\end{gathered}\]

This is a scaling by 1/2 and an anticlockwise rotation through 2π/3 about the origin. There is no translation.

examples.title: 4 · Every cube root, with principal arguments
examples.question: Solve \(z^3=27i\), using \(-\pi\le\arg z<\pi\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}27i=27e^{i\pi/2}\\z_k=3e^{i(\pi/6+2k\pi/3)},\quad k=0,1,2\\\arg z=\frac\pi6,\quad\frac{5\pi}{6},\quad-\frac\pi2\end{gathered}\]

The third unreduced angle is 3π/2; subtract a full turn. The roots have the same modulus 3 and three distinct directions.

lessons.title: Multiple angles and exact polynomial roots
lessons.summary: Use real and imaginary parts, then account for every algebraic root.
lessons.objective: Derive multiple-angle formulae and use them to solve polynomial equations completely.
lessons.before: Complete the preceding lesson. Use radians and retain exact values.
lessons.ideas:
Expand one complex power

Expand (c+is)ᵐ, set c=\(\cos \theta\) and s=\(\sin \theta\), and equate real or imaginary parts with \(\cos m\theta\) or \(\sin m\theta\). Eliminate the unwanted squared trigonometric term using \(c^{2}\)+\(s^{2}\)=1. When dividing the imaginary and real expressions, retain every non-zero-denominator restriction.

\[\begin{gathered}(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^m\\=\cos m\theta+i\sin m\theta\\\tan m\theta=\frac{\operatorname{Im}(1+it)^m}{\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^m},\quad t=\tan\theta\end{gathered}\]

Choose a useful substitution and interval

For a polynomial built from a cosine identity, try x=\(\cos \theta\) and select 0≤θ≤π, where cosine is one-to-one. For sine, use a one-to-one interval such as −π/2≤θ≤π/2. For tangent or cotangent use a single interval of length π avoiding the poles. This prevents two different angles from being mistaken for distinct polynomial roots.

Clearing a denominator creates candidates

Secant and cosecant substitutions require non-zero cosine and sine. A multiple-angle quotient may also have poles. After multiplying through, check the original equation and any divided factors. A cancelled zero factor must be considered separately.

Show completeness

Distinct valid roots equal in number to the polynomial degree account for every root. If fewer are found, use factorisation or a separate argument to identify the remaining branches and multiplicities. A trigonometric substitution covering [−1,1] does not automatically rule out other real roots.

Use coefficients for a final exact quantity

Once the whole root set is established, Viète’s formulae can give sums, products and reciprocal sums without approximating the angles. Include any scaling between polynomial roots and the requested trigonometric values.
lessons.method:
1. Expand the selected complex power and identify its real or imaginary part.
  2. Eliminate the unwanted squared function and state denominator restrictions.
  3. Choose a one-to-one angular interval for the algebraic substitution.
  4. Find every admissible angle and check distinctness and excluded cases.
  5. Use degree, multiplicity or factorisation to justify completeness.
mistakes: The imaginary part of \(i^{2}\) is zero; retain the alternating signs correctly.
A quotient identity is valid only where its denominator is non-zero.
Different angles can give the same sine or cosine value.
A trigonometric substitution does not cover every real number automatically.
Scale a root sum or product when the polynomial variable has a multiplier.

examples.title: 1 · A fourth-angle polynomial
examples.question: Derive \(\cos 4\theta\) as a polynomial in c=\(\cos \theta\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\operatorname{Re}(c+is)^4=c^4-6c^2s^2+s^4\\s^2=1-c^2\\\cos4\theta=8c^4-8c^2+1\end{gathered}\]

The imaginary terms do not contribute. Expanding after replacing \(s^{2}\) gives a whole polynomial in c.

examples.title: 2 · A quotient with a restriction
examples.question: Derive \(\tan 3\theta\) as a rational function of t=\(\tan \theta\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}(1+it)^3=(1-3t^2)+i(3t-t^3)\\\tan3\theta=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2}\end{gathered}\]

Here \(\cos \theta\)≠0 and 1−3\(t^{2}\)≠0. A zero real part would give a pole of the multiple-angle tangent rather than a value of this quotient.

examples.title: 3 · Three exact real roots
examples.question: Solve \(8x^3-6x-1=0\) in cosine form.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}x=\cos\theta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\cos3\theta=\frac12\\0\le\theta\le\pi\\\theta=\frac\pi9,\quad\frac{5\pi}{9},\quad\frac{7\pi}{9}\\x=\cos\frac\pi9,\quad\cos\frac{5\pi}{9},\quad\cos\frac{7\pi}{9}\end{gathered}\]

The three cosine values are distinct because cosine is one-to-one on the chosen interval. They are roots of a cubic, so the list is complete.

examples.title: 4 · Select all four angles
examples.question: Solve \(16x^4-16x^2+1=0\) in cosine form.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\cos4\theta=\frac12,\qquad x=\cos\theta\\\theta=\frac\pi{12},\quad\frac{5\pi}{12},\quad\frac{7\pi}{12},\quad\frac{11\pi}{12}\end{gathered}\]

Each angle lies in [0,π], and none is repeated. Four distinct roots account for the quartic. Using only the first-quadrant angles would lose the two negative roots.

lessons.title: Power identities and trigonometric integrals
lessons.summary: Reverse the multiple-angle process by pairing reciprocal powers.
lessons.objective: Express powers of sine and cosine as harmonic sums and apply them with correct scales.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Use radians and retain exact values.

Written integration extensions require integration techniques and, for Q8, the reduction-formula method. Their calculus is a prerequisite application.
lessons.ideas:
Pair opposite powers

Set \(z=e^{i\theta}\). Then z+\(z^{-1}\)=2cos θ and z−\(z^{-1}\)=2i \(\sin \theta\). Expand a suitable power and pair terms with exponents j and −j. Their sum gives a cosine; their difference gives a sine. This is a derivation from complex numbers rather than a quoted power-reduction formula.

\[\begin{gathered}z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\\z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\\\cos^m\theta=\frac{(z+z^{-1})^m}{2^m}\\\sin^m\theta=\frac{(z-z^{-1})^m}{(2i)^m}\end{gathered}\]

Track the power of i

The denominator for a sine power includes \(i^{m}\). For an even power it can be negative. For an odd power it combines with the paired sine terms. Check the final identity at a simple angle and against its symmetry, while recognising that spot checks alone are not a proof.

Products and quotients

Mixed powers use a product of the two Laurent expansions. For a quotient, derive numerator and denominator separately, then state where the original denominator is non-zero. Do not cancel a restriction that came from the original function.

Integrate the complete identity

Every non-zero-frequency sine or cosine has a frequency factor in its primitive. Under u=kx the differential contributes 1/k and both limits change. Include a constant term, symmetry factor or algebraic substitution only when justified by the stated integral.
lessons.method:
1. Choose z+\(z^{-1}\), z−\(z^{-1}\) or their product to match the powers.
  2. Expand and pair positive and negative exponents.
  3. Divide by the full power of 2 and i.
  4. For a quotient preserve its denominator restrictions.
  5. For integration transform the variable, scale and endpoints together.
mistakes: Dividing a sine expansion by 2ᵐ alone loses \(i^{m}\).
Pair equal-magnitude positive and negative exponents.
Odd and even powers have different harmonic patterns.
The primitive of cos(kx) contains 1/k.
A quotient identity does not remove a pole of the original function.

examples.title: 1 · An odd cosine power
examples.question: Use a complex expansion to express \(\cos^{5}\theta\) as a harmonic sum.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}(z+z^{-1})^5\\=z^5+5z^3+10z+10z^{-1}+5z^{-3}+z^{-5}\\\cos^5\theta=\frac{10\cos\theta+5\cos3\theta+\cos5\theta}{16}\end{gathered}\]

Each paired power contributes twice its cosine. Divide the full expansion by 2⁵.

examples.title: 2 · A mixed power and a definite integral
examples.question: Find the harmonic form of \(\sin^{2}\theta\) \(\cos^{2}\theta\) and integrate it from 0 to π/8.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta=\frac{1-\cos4\theta}{8}\\\int_0^{\pi/8}\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta\\=\left[\frac\theta8-\frac{\sin4\theta}{32}\right]_0^{\pi/8}\\=\frac\pi{64}-\frac1{32}\end{gathered}\]

The Laurent product (z−\(z^{-1}\))²(z+\(z^{-1}\))² gives the identity after division by −16. The negative denominator comes from \(i^{2}\).

examples.title: 3 · A complete quotient identity
examples.question: Express \(\tan^{4}\theta\) using only \(\cos 2\theta\), \(\cos 4\theta\) and constants.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}8\sin^4\theta=3-4\cos2\theta+\cos4\theta\\8\cos^4\theta=3+4\cos2\theta+\cos4\theta\\\tan^4\theta=\frac{3-4\cos2\theta+\cos4\theta}{3+4\cos2\theta+\cos4\theta}\end{gathered}\]

The denominator equals 8co\(s^{4}\)θ, so the original condition \(\cos \theta\)≠0 remains necessary.

examples.title: 4 · A frequency changes the integral
examples.question: Evaluate \(\int_0^{\pi/8}\cos^4(2x)\,dx\) using a derived harmonic identity.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\cos^4u=\frac38+\frac12\cos2u+\frac18\cos4u\\u=2x,\qquad0\le u\le\frac\pi4\\\int_0^{\pi/8}\cos^4(2x)\,dx\\=\frac12\left[\frac{3u}{8}+\frac{\sin2u}{4}+\frac{\sin4u}{32}\right]_0^{\pi/4}\\=\frac{3\pi}{64}+\frac18\end{gathered}\]

The factor 1/2 from dx=du/2 is independent of the harmonic coefficients.

lessons.title: Roots of unity, root polygons and parameter cases
lessons.summary: Use the whole root set, with exclusions and multiplicities.
lessons.objective: Apply root-of-unity structure to products, geometry and equations depending on parameters.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Use radians and retain exact values.

Q22 also uses a 3×3 determinant: review determinants. For root sums and products, use the coefficients of the complete polynomial.
lessons.ideas:
The root-of-unity filter

For \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/m}\), the mth roots of unity are 1,ω,…,\(ω^{m-1}\). Their powers make a finite geometric progression.

\[\begin{gathered}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\omega^{jk}\\=\begin{cases}m,&m\mid j,\\0,&m\nmid j.\end{cases}\end{gathered}\]

In the divisible case every term is 1; in the other case the geometric numerator is zero and the denominator is non-zero. This explains exactly which power sums survive.

Removing a subset

An equation obtained by multiplying by zᵈ−1 may introduce all of the dth roots of unity. Exclude them from the enlarged set, and verify the remaining roots in the original polynomial. Factorisation also makes multiplicities explicit.

Products from factorisation

\[\begin{gathered}1+x+\cdots+x^{m-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(x-\omega^k)\\\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(1-\omega^k)=m\end{gathered}\]

The root 1 is omitted from this product. For reciprocal sums, pair conjugate non-real roots or differentiate a suitable polynomial identity. State why every denominator is non-zero.

Geometry about the right centre

The roots of (z−c)ᵐ=A lie on a circle centred at c. Find the unshifted roots and then add c to each one. Their angles before translation describe the vectors z−c. To find the nearest vertex to a point d, minimise |z−d|² over every vertex; do not assume a labelled root is nearest without comparing directions.

Parameters and repeated roots

A substitution u=\(z^{m}\) can reduce the degree. Roots u on the unit circle give roots z on the unit circle, but coincident u-values can produce repeated z-roots. Treat the equality endpoints separately from the interval with distinct roots.
lessons.method:
1. Write the complete roots or factor the reduced equation.
  2. Separate an excluded subset before counting roots.
  3. Use the unity filter or polynomial coefficients for sums and products.
  4. For geometry translate the full set and compare squared distances.
  5. Handle parameter endpoints and repeated roots separately.
mistakes: The root 1 is excluded from products over nontrivial unity roots.
Do not retain roots introduced by multiplying an equation.
Angles from a translated centre are not arguments from the origin.
All roots on a circle need not be distinct.
The nearest vertex must be justified, not inferred from a sketch alone.

examples.title: 1 · Exclude the introduced roots
examples.question: Find every root of \(z^4+1=0\) by considering eighth roots of unity.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}(z^4-1)(z^4+1)=z^8-1\\z=e^{ik\pi/4},\qquad k=1,3,5,7\end{gathered}\]

The even indices are exactly the fourth roots of unity and must be removed. The remaining four distinct roots satisfy the original quartic.

examples.title: 2 · Translate the entire square
examples.question: Solve \((z+2-i)^4=81\) in Cartesian form.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}v=z+2-i,\qquad v^4=81\\v=3,\quad3i,\quad-3,\quad-3i\\z=1+i,\quad-2+4i,\quad-5+i,\quad-2-2i\end{gathered}\]

The square has centre −2+i and circumradius 3. Add the centre after finding the four unshifted roots.

examples.title: 3 · A product and a reciprocal sum
examples.question: Let \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/5}\). Find \(\prod_{k=1}^4(1-\omega^k)\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^4(1-\omega^k)^{-1}\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\prod_{k=1}^4(x-\omega^k)=1+x+x^2+x^3+x^4\\\prod_{k=1}^4(1-\omega^k)=5\\\frac1{1-\omega^k}+\frac1{1-\omega^{-k}}=1\\\sum_{k=1}^4\frac1{1-\omega^k}=2\end{gathered}\]

There are two conjugate pairs, and none contains 1. Each pair contributes 1 to the reciprocal sum.

examples.title: 4 · A full parameter interval and its endpoints
examples.question: For real a, when do all roots of \(z^6-2az^3+1=0\) have modulus 1? When are they distinct?
examples.solution: \[\begin{gathered}u=z^3,\qquad u^2-2au+1=0\\u=a\pm\sqrt{a^2-1}\\\text{All roots have modulus 1: }-1\le a\le1\\\text{Six distinct roots: }-1Inside the interval the two u-values are distinct conjugates of modulus 1. Each has three distinct cube roots, and the two families do not overlap. At a=1 the polynomial is (\(z^{3}\)−1)²; at a=−1 it is (\(z^{3}\)+1)². Each endpoint has three distinct roots, each of multiplicity two. Outside the interval the real reciprocal u-values cannot both have modulus 1.

lessons.title: Finite, binomial and convergent complex sums
lessons.summary: Sum the complex expression first, then take its real or imaginary part.
lessons.objective: Derive complete trigonometric sums, including exceptional ratios and convergence conditions.
lessons.before:
Complete the preceding lesson. Use radians and retain exact values.

Q52 uses rectangle bounds; Q57–58 differentiate a finite sum. These prerequisite links do not add new requirements to the complex-number identities.
lessons.ideas:
Identify first term, ratio and number of terms

\[\begin{gathered}\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}aq^r=a\frac{1-q^n}{1-q}\quad(q\ne1)\\\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}a=na\quad(q=1)\end{gathered}\]

For a trigonometric progression, encode the phase and frequency in the first term and ratio. Sum before taking the real or imaginary part. If the ratio is 1, evaluate the finite sum directly; the quotient formula has an excluded denominator.

Rewrite a complex difference carefully

\[\begin{gathered}1-e^{iu}=-2ie^{iu/2}\sin\frac u2\end{gathered}\]

This identity separates a phase from a sine factor. The sine factor can be negative, so an exponential times a real sine quotient is not automatically a polar form with positive modulus. State the necessary non-zero-sine restrictions and then handle exceptional angles directly.

Binomial coefficients and weights

\[\begin{gathered}\sum_{r=0}^n\binom nr z^r=(1+z)^n\\\sum_{r=0}^nr\binom nr z^r=nz(1+z)^{n-1}\end{gathered}\]

The weighted identity follows by differentiating the finite polynomial and multiplying by z. Alternatively use r times n-choose-r = n times (n−1)-choose-(r−1), then change the index. Derivatives of finite trigonometric sums can be taken term by term; track the sign when differentiating a cosine.

Infinite sums need a modulus test

\[\begin{gathered}\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(\rho e^{i\theta})^r=\frac{\rho e^{i\theta}}{1-\rho e^{i\theta}},\quad|\rho|<1\end{gathered}\]

The tail tends to zero because the ratio has modulus less than 1. Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate to extract both components. A finite cancellation at a root of unity does not justify an infinite geometric sum of modulus 1.
lessons.method:
1. Encode the actual first term, ratio, phase and term count.
  2. Use a finite geometric or binomial identity with its restrictions.
  3. Simplify the full complex expression before taking real and imaginary parts.
  4. Evaluate excluded ratios or angles directly.
  5. For an infinite sum prove the ratio modulus is less than 1.
mistakes: A sum from r=0 to n−1 has n terms; a sum to n has n+1.
A phase shift belongs in the complex first term.
Evaluate the ratio-one case directly.
An infinite geometric series needs |q|<1.
Differentiating cos(rθ) produces a negative sign and a factor r.

examples.title: 1 · A finite non-unit ratio
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{k=0}^{5}(1+i)^k\) in Cartesian form.
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sum_{k=0}^{5}(1+i)^k=\frac{1-(1+i)^6}{1-(1+i)}\\(1+i)^6=-8i\\\frac{1+8i}{-i}=-8+i\end{gathered}\]

The modulus √2 is greater than 1, but that does not prevent summing six terms. It would prevent the corresponding infinite geometric sum.

examples.title: 2 · Extract both components of a trigonometric sum
examples.question: Find \(\sum_{r=1}^{4}\cos(r\pi/3)\) and \(\sum_{r=1}^{4}\sin(r\pi/3)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}q=e^{i\pi/3},\qquad\sum_{r=1}^4q^r=\frac{q(1-q^4)}{1-q}\\=-\frac32+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i\end{gathered}\]

The two requested sums are respectively the real and imaginary parts. Direct exact-angle values provide a separate check.

examples.title: 3 · A weighted binomial sum
examples.question: Find the real and imaginary parts of \(\sum_{r=0}^{4}r\binom4r i^r\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}\sum_{r=0}^4r\binom4r z^r=4z(1+z)^3\\4i(1+i)^3=-8-8i\end{gathered}\]

The cosine-weighted sum at angle π/2 is −8, and the sine-weighted sum is −8. The zero-index term contributes zero.

examples.title: 4 · Two convergent infinite sums
examples.question: Find \(C=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}3^{-r}\cos(r\pi/3)\) and \(S=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}3^{-r}\sin(r\pi/3)\).
examples.solution:
\[\begin{gathered}q=\frac13e^{i\pi/3},\qquad|q|=\frac13<1\\C+iS=\frac q{1-q}=\frac1{14}+\frac{3\sqrt3}{14}i\\C=\frac1{14},\qquad S=\frac{3\sqrt3}{14}\end{gathered}\]

The conjugate denominator gives a real positive denominator. The modulus condition justifies taking the infinite geometric sum.

questions.title: A scaled secant equation
questions.prompt_html:
Use exact values throughout.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cos5\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\cos\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Hence solve \(x^5+20x^4-320x^2+1024=0\), writing every root as \(2\sec(q\pi)\).

    [4]

  3. Deduce the exact sum of the five secant values appearing in part (b).

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{5}=\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 5\theta=c^{5} - 10 c^{3} u^{2} + 5 c u^{4}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 5\theta=16 \cos^{5}\theta - 20 \cos^{3}\theta + 5 \cos\theta.\]

(b)

Put \(x=2\sec\theta\). Multiplication of \(\cos5\theta=-\tfrac12\) by \(2x^5\) produces the given polynomial.

\[5\theta=2k\pi\pm\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]

Choose \(0\leq\theta\leq\pi\), where cosine is one-to-one. The five angles are

\[\frac{2 \pi}{15},\ \frac{4 \pi}{15},\ \frac{8 \pi}{15},\ \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ \frac{14 \pi}{15}.\]

None has zero cosine. These give five distinct roots of a degree-five polynomial, so no other roots remain.

(c)

The monic polynomial has root sum \(-20\). Each polynomial root is twice its corresponding secant value.

\[\sum\sec\theta=\frac{-20}{2}=-10.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the fifth power and take its real part.

(b)

Use \(\cos\theta=2/x\), not \(1/x\).

(c)

Use the coefficient of \(x^4\).

questions.title: A shifted sine progression
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer.

  1. For \(z e0\) and \(z^3 e1\), express \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}z^{3r+1}\) as a single quotient.

    [2]

  2. Use \(z=e^{i heta}\) to obtain a product-form expression for \(\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\sin((3r+1) heta)\), when \(\sin(3 heta/2) e0\).

    [4]

  3. Evaluate the sum directly when \( heta=2m\pi/3\), where \(m\) is an integer.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

This is a geometric progression with first term \(z\) and ratio \(z^3\), so

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}z^{3r+1}=\frac{z(1-z^{3n})}{1-z^3}.\]

(b)

Use \(1-e^{iu}=-2ie^{iu/2}\sin(u/2)\). The complex sum becomes

\[e^{i(3n-1)\theta/2}\frac{\sin(3n\theta/2)}{\sin(3\theta/2)}.\]

Its imaginary part is the required sum:

\[\frac{\sin{\left(\frac{3 n \theta}{2} \right)} \sin{\left(\frac{\theta \left(3 n - 1\right)}{2} \right)}}{\sin{\left(\frac{3 \theta}{2} \right)}}\]

(c)

Each angle \((3r+1)\theta\) differs from \(\theta\) by \(2rm\pi\); all terms are equal.

questions.title: A quotient of sixth powers
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), with \(\cos\theta\ne0\).

  1. By expanding \((z-z^{-1})^6\) and \((z+z^{-1})^6\), express \(\tan^6\theta\) as a quotient involving only \(\cos2\theta,\cos4\theta,\cos6\theta\) and constants.

    [7]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{6}=z^{6} - 6 z^{4} + 15 z^{2} - 20 + \frac{15}{z^{2}} - \frac{6}{z^{4}} + \frac{1}{z^{6}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{6}i^{6}\). This gives

\[\sin^{6}\theta=- \frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}.\]

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{6}=z^{6} + 6 z^{4} + 15 z^{2} + 20 + \frac{15}{z^{2}} + \frac{6}{z^{4}} + \frac{1}{z^{6}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{6}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{6}\theta=\frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}.\]

Divide the two identities. The denominator is \(32\cos^6\theta\), so the stated exclusion is exactly what is needed.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Remember \(i^6=-1\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Relate the sums and differences of z and its inverse to cosine and sine.
Handle the sign from the sixth power of i.
Form the quotient and state the correct domain.

questions.title: A sine-power integral after substitution
questions.prompt_html:
The identity must be obtained by a complex-number method.

  1. Use \((z-z^{-1})^4\), where \(z=e^{i\theta}\), to express \(\sin^4\theta\) in multiple-angle form.

    [5]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt3/2}\frac{x^4}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{4}=z^{4} - 4 z^{2} + 6 - \frac{4}{z^{2}} + \frac{1}{z^{4}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{4}i^{4}\). This gives

\[\sin^{4}\theta=- \frac{\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{2} + \frac{\cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{8} + \frac{3}{8}.\]

(b)

Put \(x=\sin\theta\). The limits are \(0\) and \(\pi/3\); cosine is non-negative there, so the square root cancels the Jacobian.

\[\int_0^{\sqrt3/2}\frac{x^4}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}\,dx=\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^4\theta\,d\theta.\]
\[\left[\frac{3 \theta}{8} - \frac{\sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{4} + \frac{\sin{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{32}\right]_0^{\pi/3}=- \frac{9 \sqrt{3}}{64} + \frac{\pi}{8}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Group conjugate powers of z.

(b)

The Jacobian cancels the denominator, rather than adding another sine power.

marking_criteria.description_html: Apply the substitution and change both limits.

questions.title: Six cotangent roots
questions.prompt_html:
Give a complete set of roots, without repetitions.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to obtain an expression for \(\cot6\theta\) in terms of \(u=\cot\theta\).

    [6]

  2. Hence solve \(x^{6} + 6 \sqrt{3} x^{5} - 15 x^{4} - 20 \sqrt{3} x^{3} + 15 x^{2} + 6 \sqrt{3} x - 1=0\), expressing all roots as \(\cot(q\pi)\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\cot6\theta=\frac{u^{6} - 15 u^{4} + 15 u^{2} - 1}{6 u^{5} - 20 u^{3} + 6 u}.\]

(b)

\[x=\cot\theta,\quad \theta=\frac{5 \pi}{36},\ \frac{11 \pi}{36},\ \frac{17 \pi}{36},\ \frac{23 \pi}{36},\ \frac{29 \pi}{36},\ \frac{35 \pi}{36}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(x=\cot heta\). For \(\sin heta e0\),

\[(x+i)^{6}= rac{\cos 6 heta+i\sin 6 heta}{\sin^{6} heta}.\]

The binomial expansion gives

\[\operatorname{Re}(x+i)^{6}=x^{6} - 15 x^{4} + 15 x^{2} - 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(x+i)^{6}=6 x^{5} - 20 x^{3} + 6 x.\]

Dividing real by imaginary parts is valid when \(\sin 6 heta e0\):

\[\cot 6 heta= rac{x^{6} - 15 x^{4} + 15 x^{2} - 1}{6 x^{5} - 20 x^{3} + 6 x}.\]

(b)

The equation is \(N(x)+\sqrt3D(x)=0\), where \(N+iD=(x+i)^6\). These polynomials cannot both vanish for real \(x\), since \(x+i e0\). Division therefore loses no solution.

\[\cot6 heta=-\sqrt3,\qquad 6 heta= rac{5\pi}{6}+k\pi.\]
\[ heta= rac{5\pi}{36}+ rac{k\pi}{6},\quad k=0,\ldots,5.\]

All angles lie in \((0,\pi)\), where cotangent is injective. The six distinct roots exhaust the degree.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand \((u+i)^6\).

(b)

Check that the numerator and denominator do not have a common real zero.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give all six roots and justify completeness.

questions.title: Harmonics and a ninth-power integral
questions.prompt_html:
For integers \(n\geq0\), let \(J_n=\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^n\theta\,d\theta\).

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\sin^7\theta\) as a linear combination of \(\sin\theta,\sin3\theta,\sin5\theta,\sin7\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Prove that, for \(n\geq2\), \(nJ_n=(n-1)J_{n-2}-\tfrac12(\sqrt3/2)^{n-1}\).

    [4]

  3. Use parts (a) and (b) to find \(J_9\) exactly.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{7}=z^{7} - 7 z^{5} + 21 z^{3} - 35 z + \frac{35}{z} - \frac{21}{z^{3}} + \frac{7}{z^{5}} - \frac{1}{z^{7}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{7}i^{7}\). This gives

\[\sin^{7}\theta=\frac{35 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{21 \sin{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{\sin{\left(7 \theta \right)}}{64}.\]

(b)

Integrate \(\sin^{n-1}\theta\sin\theta\) by parts with \(v=-\cos\theta\):

\[J_n=[-\sin^{n-1}\theta\cos\theta]_0^{\pi/3}+(n-1)\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^{n-2}\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta.\]

The boundary term is \(-\tfrac12(\sqrt3/2)^{n-1}\). Use \(\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta\), then move \((n-1)J_n\) to the left.

(c)

Integrating the harmonics in (a) gives

\[J_7=\left[- \frac{35 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{7 \cos{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{7 \cos{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{320} + \frac{\cos{\left(7 \theta \right)}}{448}\right]_0^{\pi/3}=\frac{289}{4480}.\]
\[9J_9=8J_7-\frac12\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^8.\]
\[J_9=\frac{6413}{161280}.\]

The final value is rational because the endpoint cosine values in all the odd harmonics are rational.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The seventh power of \(2i\sin\theta\) has a minus sign.

(b)

The upper boundary term is not zero.

(c)

First evaluate J7 from the harmonic identity; then use just one reduction step.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the identity to introduce J(n-2) and J(n).

questions.title: A negative power equation
questions.prompt_html:
A nonzero complex number \(z\) satisfies \(z^{-3}=8i\).

  1. Find every possible value of \(z\) in exponential form, with \(-\pi\leq\arg z\lt\pi\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Take a reciprocal first: \(z^3=1/(8i)=-i/8\). Its modulus is \(1/8\) and an argument is \(-\pi/2\).

\[|z|=\frac12,\qquad \arg z=-\frac\pi6+\frac{2k\pi}{3},\quad k=0,1,2.\]

Reduce the last angle \(7\pi/6\) by \(2\pi\), obtaining \(-5\pi/6\). All three values are required; choosing only a principal cube root would omit solutions.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Invert the right-hand side before taking roots.

marking_criteria.description_html: Take the modulus root and obtain all argument values.
Give all roots in the required interval.

questions.title: A nested polynomial and its real roots
questions.prompt_html:
Work over the complex numbers except where real roots are requested.

  1. Find all six roots of \(w^6=1\) in exponential form. Identify its real roots.

    [2]

  2. Use de Moivre’s theorem to prove \(\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta\).

    [4]

  3. Hence find all real roots of \(64(4x^3-3x)^6-1=0\), and state the number of non-real roots counted with multiplicity.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[w=e^{ik\pi/3},\ k=0,\ldots,5;\quad w=1,-1\text{ are real}.\]

(b)

\[\cos3\theta=4\cos^3\theta-3\cos\theta.\]

(c)

\[x=\cos\theta,\quad\theta=\frac{\pi}{9},\ \frac{2 \pi}{9},\ \frac{4 \pi}{9},\ \frac{5 \pi}{9},\ \frac{7 \pi}{9},\ \frac{8 \pi}{9};\quad12\text{ non-real roots}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

All roots have modulus 1; their arguments differ by \(\pi/3\). A root is real only at angles 0 and \(\pi\).

(b)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{3}=\cos 3\theta+i\sin 3\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 3\theta=c^{3} - 3 c u^{2}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 3\theta=4 \cos^{3}\theta - 3 \cos\theta.\]

(c)

For real \(x\), the real quantity \(2(4x^3-3x)\) must be \(1\) or \(-1\). Thus \(\cos3\theta=\pm\tfrac12\).

\[\theta=\frac{\pi}{9},\ \frac{2 \pi}{9},\ \frac{4 \pi}{9},\ \frac{5 \pi}{9},\ \frac{7 \pi}{9},\ \frac{8 \pi}{9}.\]

These are six distinct roots. Each of the two real cubics has at most three roots, so all real solutions have been found. The original polynomial has degree 18; therefore 12 remaining roots are non-real, counted with multiplicity.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Locate the roots on the unit circle.

(b)

Take real parts of the cube.

(c)

The other four sixth roots of unity cannot equal a real cubic expression.

marking_criteria.description_html: Retain only the two real sixth-root branches.

questions.title: Which power sums survive?
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(z_0,z_1,z_2\) be the roots of \(z^3=8i\), and let \(S_m=z_0^m+z_1^m+z_2^m\), where \(m\) is a positive integer.

  1. Find the three roots in exponential form, using arguments in \([0,2\pi)\).

    [4]

  2. Find \(S_m\) for every positive integer \(m\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(8i=8e^{i\pi/2}\). Taking cube roots gives modulus 2 and arguments \(\pi/6,5\pi/6,3\pi/2\).

(b)

Let \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}\). Then \(z_k=2e^{i\pi/6}\omega^k\), so

\[S_m=2^me^{im\pi/6}(1+\omega^m+\omega^{2m}).\]

If \(3\mid m\), the bracket is 3. Otherwise \(\omega^m\ne1\) and its cube is 1, so the geometric sum is zero. For \(m=3q\), the surviving factor is \(2^{3q}e^{iq\pi/2}=(8i)^q\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Add multiples of \(2\pi\) before dividing by 3.

(b)

A geometric sum cancels unless the ratio is 1.

marking_criteria.description_html: Factor out a common root to the mth power.

questions.title: Eighth powers on a symmetric interval
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\).

  1. By expanding \((z+z^{-1})^8\), express \(128\cos^8\theta\) as a linear combination of \(1,\cos2\theta,\cos4\theta,\cos6\theta,\cos8\theta\).

    [6]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\cos^8(x/2)\,dx\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{8}=z^{8} + 8 z^{6} + 28 z^{4} + 56 z^{2} + 70 + \frac{56}{z^{2}} + \frac{28}{z^{4}} + \frac{8}{z^{6}} + \frac{1}{z^{8}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{8}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{8}\theta=\frac{7 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{7 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{128} + \frac{35}{128}.\]

Multiply the resulting identity by 128.

(b)

Put \(\theta=x/2\), so \(dx=2\,d\theta\). The transformed bounds are \(-\pi/6\) and \(\pi/6\).

\[2\left[\frac{35 \theta}{128} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{128} + \frac{\sin{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{96} + \frac{\sin{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{1024}\right]_{-\pi/6}^{\pi/6}=\frac{35 \pi}{192} + \frac{279 \sqrt{3}}{512}.\]

Alternatively use evenness after the change of variable; the factor 2 from the Jacobian is still required.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Pair opposite powers, keeping the middle binomial coefficient.

(b)

Distinguish the substitution factor from the symmetry factor.

marking_criteria.description_html: Relate the expression to 256 cosine to the eighth power.

questions.title: Proving and extending de Moivre
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(r\gt0\), \(\theta\in\mathbb R\), and \(z=r(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)\).

  1. Prove by mathematical induction that \(z^n=r^n(\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta)\) for every positive integer \(n\).

    [4]

  2. Deduce the corresponding formula for \(z^{-n}\), and explain the change in modulus and argument.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The formula holds for every positive integer n.

(b)

\[z^{-n}=r^{-n}(\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta).\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(n=1\), the result is the definition of \(z\). Assume the formula holds for \(n=k\). Then

\[z^{k+1}=r^{k+1}(\cos k\theta+i\sin k\theta)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta).\]
\[=r^{k+1}\{\cos k\theta\cos\theta-\sin k\theta\sin\theta+i(\sin k\theta\cos\theta+\cos k\theta\sin\theta)\}.\]

The addition formulae make the bracket equal to \(\cos((k+1)\theta)+i\sin((k+1)\theta)\). This proves the induction step. The result therefore holds for every positive integer.

(b)

Because \(r\gt0\), \(z^n\ne0\), and

\[\frac1{z^n}=r^{-n}\frac{\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta}{\cos^2n\theta+\sin^2n\theta}=r^{-n}(\cos n\theta-i\sin n\theta).\]

The modulus becomes \(r^{-n}\); an argument is \(-n\theta\), reduced modulo \(2\pi\) when a principal argument is requested.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The induction step needs the addition formulae, not the conclusion you are trying to prove.

(b)

Rationalise the reciprocal using the conjugate.

marking_criteria.description_html: Multiply by z and use both addition formulae.
Identify the k+1 case and conclude by induction.

questions.title: A quartic from a tangent equation
questions.prompt_html:
All angles are in radians.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\tan4\theta\) in terms of \(t=\tan\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Hence solve \(\sqrt{3} t^{4} + 4 t^{3} - 6 \sqrt{3} t^{2} - 4 t + \sqrt{3}=0\), giving all four roots as tangent values.

    [3]

  3. Find the exact sum of the squares of these four roots.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(t=\tan\theta\), de Moivre gives

\[(1+it)^{4}=\sec^{4}\theta(\cos 4\theta+i\sin 4\theta).\]

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{4}=t^{4} - 6 t^{2} + 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{4}=- 4 t^{3} + 4 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 4\theta=\frac{- 4 t^{3} + 4 t}{t^{4} - 6 t^{2} + 1}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 4\theta\ne0\).

(b)

The equation gives \(\tan4\theta=\sqrt3\), so

\[4\theta=\frac\pi3+k\pi,\qquad\theta=\frac\pi{12}+\frac{k\pi}4.\]

For \(k=0,1,2,3\), the four finite tangent values are distinct. If both real and imaginary parts of \((1+it)^4\) vanished, the number itself would vanish, which is impossible for real \(t\). Thus no root is lost by division.

(c)

Divide the quartic by \(\sqrt3\). Then the root sum is \(-4/\sqrt3\), and the pairwise product sum is \(-6\).

\[\sum t_j^2=\left(-\frac4{\sqrt3}\right)^2-2(-6)=\frac{52}{3}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take the ratio of imaginary to real parts.

(b)

Use one period of tangent to avoid repeating a root.

(c)

Use \(\sum t_j^2=(\sum t_j)^2-2\sum_{j\lt k}t_jt_k\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Expand the fourth power and find both parts.
Give four distinct roots and exclude invalid divisions.
Combine them to obtain the sum of squares.

questions.title: A product of three tangent values
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(t=\tan\theta\).

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\tan7\theta\) as a rational function of \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Use \(\tan7\theta=0\) to identify the six roots of \(t^6-21t^4+35t^2-7=0\).

    [2]

  3. Deduce \(\tan(\pi/7)\tan(2\pi/7)\tan(3\pi/7)\) exactly.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\tan7\theta=\frac{- t^{7} + 21 t^{5} - 35 t^{3} + 7 t}{- 7 t^{6} + 35 t^{4} - 21 t^{2} + 1}.\]

(b)

\[t=\pm\tan\frac\pi7,\quad\pm\tan\frac{2\pi}7,\quad\pm\tan\frac{3\pi}7.\]

(c)

\[\sqrt7.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(t=\tan\theta\), de Moivre gives

\[(1+it)^{7}=\sec^{7}\theta(\cos 7\theta+i\sin 7\theta).\]

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{7}=- 7 t^{6} + 35 t^{4} - 21 t^{2} + 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{7}=- t^{7} + 21 t^{5} - 35 t^{3} + 7 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 7\theta=\frac{- t^{7} + 21 t^{5} - 35 t^{3} + 7 t}{- 7 t^{6} + 35 t^{4} - 21 t^{2} + 1}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 7\theta\ne0\).

(b)

The numerator is \(-t(t^6-21t^4+35t^2-7)\). Taking \(\theta=k\pi/7\), \(k=1,\ldots,6\), gives six nonzero, distinct, finite values. The denominator cannot also vanish, by \(\cos^2(7\theta)+\sin^2(7\theta)=1\).

(c)

The three squared tangent values are roots of \(u^3-21u^2+35u-7=0\), so their product is 7. All three tangent values are positive, giving the positive square root.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Keep the odd and even binomial terms separate.

(b)

Exclude the zero tangent before dividing by it.

(c)

The sign must follow from the angle intervals.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the product of the squared roots.

questions.title: From tangent squares to cosecant squares
questions.prompt_html:
No decimal approximations should be used.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that \(\tan5\theta=(5t-10t^3+t^5)/(1-10t^2+5t^4)\), where \(t=\tan\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Deduce a quadratic with integer coefficients whose roots are \(\cot^2(\pi/5)\) and \(\cot^2(2\pi/5)\).

    [3]

  3. Find a quadratic whose roots are \(\csc^2(\pi/5)\) and \(\csc^2(2\pi/5)\), and hence find the sum of their squares.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(t=\tan\theta\), de Moivre gives

\[(1+it)^{5}=\sec^{5}\theta(\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta).\]

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{5}=5 t^{4} - 10 t^{2} + 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{5}=t^{5} - 10 t^{3} + 5 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 5\theta=\frac{t^{5} - 10 t^{3} + 5 t}{5 t^{4} - 10 t^{2} + 1}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 5\theta\ne0\).

(b)

At \(\theta=\pi/5,2\pi/5\), the nonzero tangent values satisfy \(t^4-10t^2+5=0\). Put \(u=1/t^2\), which is permitted because both tangents are nonzero.

\[u^{-2}-10u^{-1}+5=0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad5u^2-10u+1=0.\]

(c)

Use \(v=1+u\) from \(\csc^2\theta=1+\cot^2\theta\). Substitute \(u=v-1\):

\[5(v-1)^2-10(v-1)+1=5v^2-20v+16.\]

Thus \(v_1+v_2=4\) and \(v_1v_2=16/5\).

\[v_1^2+v_2^2=16-\frac{32}{5}=\frac{48}{5}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand \((1+it)^5\).

(b)

Reciprocating roots reverses the coefficients after clearing denominators.

(c)

Apply the shift after, not before, reciprocating the tangent squares.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the equation for the tangent squares.

questions.title: Alternating binomial trigonometric sums
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(0\lt\theta\lt2\pi\), and let \(n\) be a positive integer.

  1. Write \(1-e^{i\theta}\) in modulus–argument form.

    [3]

  2. Obtain expressions for \(C_n=\sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom nr\cos r\theta\) and \(S_n=\sum_{r=0}^n(-1)^r\binom nr\sin r\theta\).

    [4]

  3. Evaluate \(C_{6m+2}\) and \(S_{6m+2}\) when \(\theta=\pi/3\), where \(m\geq0\) is an integer.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[1-e^{i\theta}=e^{i\theta/2}(e^{-i\theta/2}-e^{i\theta/2})=-2i\sin(\theta/2)e^{i\theta/2}.\]

Since \(0\lt\theta/2\lt\pi\), the sine factor is positive; it is a valid modulus. The argument \(\theta/2-\pi/2\) lies in \((-\pi/2,\pi/2)\).

(b)

The binomial theorem gives \(C_n+iS_n=(1-e^{i\theta})^n\). Apply de Moivre to part (a), then equate real and imaginary parts.

\[C_n+iS_n=\left(2\sin\frac\theta2\right)^n e^{in(\theta/2-\pi/2)}.\]

(c)

Here \(1-e^{i\pi/3}=e^{-i\pi/3}\), whose \((6m+2)\)th power is \(e^{-2\pi i/3}\). Read its real and imaginary parts.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out the half-angle exponential and check the sign of the remaining real factor.

(b)

The sum starts at r=0; its cosine term is 1.

(c)

Reduce the final argument modulo \(2\pi\).

questions.title: A mixed sixth-degree trigonometric product
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\).

  1. Express \(z^j+z^{-j}\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}\) in terms of trigonometric functions for integer \(j\).

    [3]

  2. Expand \((z+z^{-1})^4(z-z^{-1})^2\) and hence express \(\sin^2\theta\cos^4\theta\) in multiple-angle form.

    [6]

  3. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^2\theta\cos^4\theta\,d\theta\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta,\qquad z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta.\]

(b)

\[\frac{\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} - \frac{\cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{1}{16}\]

(c)

\[\frac{\pi}{96}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Apply de Moivre with exponents j and -j. Cosine is even and sine is odd. Adding and subtracting the two equations gives the result.

(b)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{4}(z-z^{-1})^{2}=z^{6} + 2 z^{4} - z^{2} - 4 - \frac{1}{z^{2}} + \frac{2}{z^{4}} + \frac{1}{z^{6}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{6}i^{2}\). This gives

\[\cos^{4}\theta\sin^{2}\theta=\frac{\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} - \frac{\cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{1}{16}.\]

(c)

\[\left[\frac{\theta}{16} + \frac{\sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{\sin{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{\sin{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{192}\right]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac{\pi}{96}.\]

Each cosine term is integrated with the reciprocal of its frequency; all sine terms vanish at the lower endpoint.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use de Moivre for both positive and negative exponents.

(b)

The second factor contributes \(i^2=-1\).

(c)

Integrate each harmonic separately.

questions.title: Adding complementary sixth powers
questions.prompt_html:
Use a complex-number expansion for the first part.

  1. Express \(\cos^6\theta\) in terms of \(\cos2\theta,\cos4\theta,\cos6\theta\) and a constant.

    [5]

  2. Find the corresponding expression for \(\sin^6\theta\), and simplify their sum.

    [3]

  3. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/12}(\cos^6\theta+\sin^6\theta)\,d\theta\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}\]

(b)

\[\sin^6\theta=- \frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16},\qquad\cos^6\theta+\sin^6\theta=\frac58+\frac38\cos4\theta.\]

(c)

\[\frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{64} + \frac{5 \pi}{96}\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{6}=z^{6} + 6 z^{4} + 15 z^{2} + 20 + \frac{15}{z^{2}} + \frac{6}{z^{4}} + \frac{1}{z^{6}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{6}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{6}\theta=\frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}.\]

(b)

Replace \(\theta\) by \(\pi/2-\theta\) in part (a). The cosines of 2 and 6 times the angle change sign; the cosine of 4 times the angle does not. Adding cancels the second- and sixth-angle cosine terms.

(c)

\[\left[\frac58\theta+\frac3{32}\sin4\theta\right]_0^{\pi/12}=\frac{5\pi}{96}+\frac{3\sqrt3}{64}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the sixth power of \(z+z^{-1}\).

(b)

Use the complementary angle rather than starting another long expansion.

(c)

Only a constant and a single cosine remain.

questions.title: Zero cotangents and a product identity
questions.prompt_html:
Show why the discarded solution is not a root of the final quartic.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cot5\theta\) in terms of \(u=\cot\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Hence find the four roots of \(u^4-10u^2+5=0\) as cotangents of rational multiples of \(\pi\).

    [2]

  3. Deduce the exact value of \(\cot^2(\pi/10)\cot^2(3\pi/10)\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(x=\cot\theta\). For \(\sin\theta\ne0\),

\[(x+i)^{5}=\frac{\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta}{\sin^{5}\theta}.\]

The binomial expansion gives

\[\operatorname{Re}(x+i)^{5}=x^{5} - 10 x^{3} + 5 x,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(x+i)^{5}=5 x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 1.\]

Dividing real by imaginary parts is valid when \(\sin 5\theta\ne0\):

\[\cot 5\theta=\frac{x^{5} - 10 x^{3} + 5 x}{5 x^{4} - 10 x^{2} + 1}.\]

(b)

Use \(5\theta=\pi/2+k\pi\). The five cotangents on \((0,\pi)\) include \(\cot(\pi/2)=0\). This zero comes from the separate factor \(u\) in the numerator, whereas the quartic has constant term 5. The other four values are its roots.

(c)

The squared positive cotangents solve \(v^2-10v+5=0\). Their product is therefore 5.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take the real part over the imaginary part.

(b)

Separate the factor u before listing roots of the quartic.

(c)

Use the quadratic in the square of u.

marking_criteria.description_html: Remove zero and give all four roots.

questions.title: An eighth sine power
questions.prompt_html:
Use \(z=e^{i\theta}\).

  1. Expand \((z-z^{-1})^8\) and hence express \(128\sin^8\theta\) as a linear combination of cosines of multiple angles.

    [6]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^8\theta\,d\theta\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{8}=z^{8} - 8 z^{6} + 28 z^{4} - 56 z^{2} + 70 - \frac{56}{z^{2}} + \frac{28}{z^{4}} - \frac{8}{z^{6}} + \frac{1}{z^{8}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{8}i^{8}\). This gives

\[\sin^{8}\theta=- \frac{7 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{7 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{32} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{128} + \frac{35}{128}.\]

Multiply the identity by 128.

(b)

\[\left[\frac{35 \theta}{128} - \frac{7 \sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{128} - \frac{\sin{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{96} + \frac{\sin{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{1024}\right]_0^{\pi/6}=- \frac{169 \sqrt{3}}{2048} + \frac{35 \pi}{768}.\]

Keep the exact trigonometric values until the final simplification; the small result is a difference of larger exact terms.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Here \(i^8=1\), but alternating binomial signs remain.

(b)

Avoid premature decimal rounding.

questions.title: Cube-root algebra and a rotated square
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/3}\) and \(u=1-\omega\).

  1. Give \(\omega\) in Cartesian form, and show that \(1+\omega+\omega^2=0\).

    [2]

  2. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\det\begin{pmatrix}1&2\omega&3\omega^2\\3\omega^2&1&2\omega\\2\omega&3\omega^2&1\end{pmatrix}\).

    [4]

  3. Find all roots of \(z^4=u^4\) in exponential form, with principal arguments in \([-\pi,\pi)\).

    [4]

  4. Sketch the four roots on an Argand diagram. Identify the root nearest to the point representing 2, and find the exact distance.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Use the cosine and sine of \(2\pi/3\). Since \(\omega^3=1\) and \(\omega\ne1\), division of \(\omega^3-1=(\omega-1)(\omega^2+\omega+1)\) proves the sum identity.

(b)

Expand the determinant using the six signed products:

\[1+8\omega^3+27\omega^6-6\omega^3-6\omega^3-6\omega^3=1+8+27-18=18.\]

Here \(\omega^3=\omega^6=1\).

(c)

\[u=\frac32-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i=\sqrt3e^{-i\pi/6}.\]

The equation \((z/u)^4=1\) gives \(z=u i^k\), \(k=0,1,2,3\). Add multiples of \(\pi/2\) to \(-\pi/6\), then reduce to the requested interval.

(d)

The points form a square on \(|z|=\sqrt3\), centred at the origin. For a point on this circle,

\[|z-2|^2=|z|^2+4-4\operatorname{Re}z=7-4\operatorname{Re}z.\]

The real parts of the four roots are \(3/2,\sqrt3/2,-3/2,-\sqrt3/2\). The largest is \(3/2\), belonging to \(u\). Hence the smallest squared distance is \(7-6=1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor the difference of cubes.

(b)

Use powers of omega to simplify after expanding.

(c)

Divide by u before using fourth roots of unity.

(d)

All roots have the same modulus, so nearest to 2 means largest real part.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the modulus and argument of u.
Give all four roots with correct arguments.

questions.title: Seven roots and two exact products
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(\omega=e^{2\pi i/7}\).

  1. Write down all seventh roots of unity and show that \(\sum_{k=0}^6\omega^{5k}=0\).

    [3]

  2. Factor \(1+x+\cdots+x^6\) over the complex numbers and hence find \(\prod_{k=1}^6(1-\omega^k)\).

    [4]

  3. Using conjugate pairs, find \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^6\frac1{1-\omega^k}\).

    [4]

  4. Let \(v_k=2-2\omega^k\), \(k=1,\ldots,6\). Find \(\prod_{k=1}^6v_k\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^6v_k^{-1}\).

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[1,\omega,\ldots,\omega^6;\qquad\sum_{k=0}^6\omega^{5k}=0.\]

(b)

\[1+x+\cdots+x^6=\prod_{k=1}^6(x-\omega^k),\qquad\prod_{k=1}^6(1-\omega^k)=7.\]

(c)

\[3.\]

(d)

\[\prod v_k=448,\qquad\sum v_k^{-1}=\frac32.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The roots are \(e^{2\pi ik/7}\), \(k=0,\ldots,6\). The ratio \(\omega^5\ne1\), but \((\omega^5)^7=1\). The geometric-series formula therefore has zero numerator and nonzero denominator.

(b)

Factor \(x^7-1\), then remove the factor \(x-1\). The remaining six distinct roots are precisely the nontrivial seventh roots, and both sides are monic of degree 6. Substitute \(x=1\); the left side is a sum of seven ones.

(c)

Pair \(k\) with \(7-k\). Writing \(a=\omega^k\), note that \(\omega^{7-k}=a^{-1}\) and \(a\ne1\).

\[\frac1{1-a}+\frac1{1-a^{-1}}=\frac1{1-a}+\frac{a}{a-1}=1.\]

There are three such pairs, giving 3.

(d)

There are six factors in the product, but each reciprocal is multiplied by just one factor of one half:

\[\prod v_k=2^6\cdot7=448,\qquad\sum v_k^{-1}=\frac12\cdot3=\frac32.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The exponent 5 permutes the seventh roots; it does not change their sum.

(b)

Use the quotient polynomial before substituting x=1.

(c)

Each reciprocal pair sums to 1, not 0.

(d)

Apply the scale factor differently to products and reciprocal sums.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use a geometric sum with ratio omega to the fifth.
Scale the product by 2 to the sixth.
Scale the reciprocal sum by one half.

questions.title: Evaluating a cubic at a trigonometric value
questions.prompt_html:
The polynomial value is to be obtained without approximating the angle.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cos6\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\cos\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Express \(\cos6\theta\) instead as a polynomial in \(\sin\theta\).

    [2]

  3. Find \(16v^3-24v^2+9v\) exactly when \(v=\cos^2(\pi/9)\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{6}=\cos 6\theta+i\sin 6\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 6\theta=c^{6} - 15 c^{4} u^{2} + 15 c^{2} u^{4} - u^{6}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 6\theta=32 \cos^{6}\theta - 48 \cos^{4}\theta + 18 \cos^{2}\theta - 1.\]

(b)

The polynomial in part (a) contains only even cosine powers. Replace \(\cos^2\theta\) by \(1-\sin^2\theta\) and expand.

\[\cos6\theta=1-18\sin^2\theta+48\sin^4\theta-32\sin^6\theta.\]

(c)

Put \(\theta=\pi/9\) in part (a). Then \(\cos6\theta=\cos(2\pi/3)=-1/2\), so

\[32v^3-48v^2+18v-1=-\frac12.\]
\[16v^3-24v^2+9v=\frac14.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the sixth power and take real parts.

(b)

Do not change the sign as though 6 were a multiple of 4.

(c)

Compare the cubic with half the multiple-angle polynomial.

questions.title: A cubic, exact tangents and reciprocal squares
questions.prompt_html:
This is one complete question; there is no alternative option.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to derive the triple-angle formula for tangent.

    [5]

  2. Solve \(t^3+3t^2-3t-1=0\), expressing the three roots as \(\tan(q\pi)\) with \(0\lt q\lt1\).

    [3]

  3. Find the exact real values of these three tangent values.

    [4]

  4. If the roots are \(t_1,t_2,t_3\), evaluate \(t_1^{-2}+t_2^{-2}+t_3^{-2}\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\tan3\theta=\frac{3t-t^3}{1-3t^2},\qquad t=\tan\theta.\]

(b)

\[t=\tan\frac\pi4,\quad\tan\frac{7\pi}{12},\quad\tan\frac{11\pi}{12}.\]

(c)

\[1,\quad-2-\sqrt3,\quad-2+\sqrt3\text{ respectively}.\]

(d)

\[15.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(t=\tan\theta\), de Moivre gives

\[(1+it)^{3}=\sec^{3}\theta(\cos 3\theta+i\sin 3\theta).\]

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{3}=1 - 3 t^{2},\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{3}=- t^{3} + 3 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 3\theta=\frac{- t^{3} + 3 t}{1 - 3 t^{2}}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 3\theta\ne0\).

(b)

The equation is equivalent to \(\tan3\theta=-1\), giving \(3\theta=3\pi/4+k\pi\). The three angles in \((0,\pi)\) are those listed. They are finite and distinct. Simultaneous zero numerator and denominator would make \((1+it)^3=0\), which is impossible for real \(t\).

(c)

\[t^3+3t^2-3t-1=(t-1)(t^2+4t+1).\]

The roots are \(1,-2\pm\sqrt3\). The angle \(7\pi/12\) lies just beyond \(\pi/2\), so its tangent is less than \(-1\); hence it gives \(-2-\sqrt3\). The angle \(11\pi/12\) gives the negative root between \(-1\) and 0.

(d)

None is zero. Their product is 1, pairwise-product sum is \(-3\), and sum is \(-3\). Therefore the reciprocal roots have sum \(-3\) and pairwise-product sum \(-3\).

\[\sum t_j^{-2}=(-3)^2-2(-3)=15.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Separate real and imaginary parts of a cube.

(b)

Use the negative tangent equation.

(c)

Factor using the obvious root 1; then assign the two negative roots by their angle intervals.

(d)

Use root sums for the reciprocal polynomial.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give three distinct roots without invalid division.
Match each exact value to its angle.
Obtain reciprocal root sum and pairwise sum.

questions.title: A mixed eighth-degree product
questions.prompt_html:
Use de Moivre’s theorem to obtain the identity needed for the integral.

  1. By considering \((z-z^{-1})^6(z+z^{-1})^2\), express \(\sin^6\theta\cos^2\theta\) in multiple-angle form.

    [6]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt2}x^6\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{2}(z-z^{-1})^{6}=z^{8} - 4 z^{6} + 4 z^{4} + 4 z^{2} - 10 + \frac{4}{z^{2}} + \frac{4}{z^{4}} - \frac{4}{z^{6}} + \frac{1}{z^{8}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{8}i^{6}\). This gives

\[\cos^{2}\theta\sin^{6}\theta=- \frac{\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} - \frac{\cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} - \frac{\cos{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{128} + \frac{5}{128}.\]

(b)

Put \(x=2\sin\theta\), with \(0\leq\theta\leq\pi/4\). Then \(\sqrt{4-x^2}=2\cos\theta\) and \(dx=2\cos\theta\,d\theta\).

\[\int_0^{\sqrt2}x^6\sqrt{4-x^2}\,dx=256\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin^6\theta\cos^2\theta\,d\theta.\]
\[=256\left[\frac{5 \theta}{128} - \frac{\sin{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{\sin{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{128} + \frac{\sin{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{192} - \frac{\sin{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{1024}\right]_0^{\pi/4}=- \frac{16}{3} + \frac{5 \pi}{2}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The total degree is eight; group powers through z to the eighth.

(b)

The total scale factor is 2 to the eighth.

marking_criteria.description_html: Pair opposite powers and handle i to the sixth.

questions.title: When all four roots lie on a circle
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(a\) be real. Consider \(z^4+2az^2+1=0\).

  1. Find the set of values of \(a\) for which every root has modulus 1.

    [4]

  2. Within this set, determine when there are four distinct roots. Describe both endpoint cases.

    [3]

  3. Find all roots when \(a=1/2\), and explain their relationship to the sixth roots of unity.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[-1\leq a\leq1.\]

(b)

\[-1\lt a\lt1;\quad a=-1:\ z=\pm1\text{ each twice};\quad a=1:\ z=\pm i\text{ each twice}.\]

(c)

\[z=e^{ik\pi/3},\qquad k=1,2,4,5.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(w=z^2\). The two w-roots satisfy \(w^2+2aw+1=0\). If \(|a|\leq1\), they are \(-a\pm i\sqrt{1-a^2}\), both of modulus 1. Their square roots also have modulus 1.

Conversely, if all z-roots have modulus 1, so do both w-roots. Their sum is \(-2a\), so the triangle inequality gives \(2|a|\leq2\). Thus \(|a|\leq1\).

(b)

For \(-1\lt a\lt1\), the two w-roots are distinct and nonzero, and each gives two square roots; the two pairs cannot overlap. At \(a=-1\), the polynomial is \((z^2-1)^2\). At \(a=1\), it is \((z^2+1)^2\).

(c)

The equation becomes \(z^4+z^2+1=0\). Multiplication by \(z^2-1\) gives \(z^6-1=0\), but \(z=\pm1\) were introduced by that multiplication and do not satisfy the quartic. The other four sixth roots are the required roots.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Square the roots first; use a converse as well as a construction.

(b)

Distinguish distinct values from roots counted with multiplicity.

(c)

Multiplication by z squared minus 1 introduces two values to remove.

marking_criteria.description_html: Reduce to a quadratic in z squared.
Prove necessity, for example by the triangle inequality.
Give all four roots and their interpretation.

questions.title: Four nonzero roots from tan six theta
questions.prompt_html:
Put \(t=\tan\theta\).

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\tan6\theta\) in terms of \(t\).

    [5]

  2. Hence identify the four roots of \(3t^4-10t^2+3=0\) as tangent values.

    [2]

  3. Find \(\sum_jt_j^2\) and \(\prod_jt_j\) for these four roots.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

For \(t=\tan\theta\), de Moivre gives

\[(1+it)^{6}=\sec^{6}\theta(\cos 6\theta+i\sin 6\theta).\]

Expanding gives the following real and imaginary parts:

\[\operatorname{Re}(1+it)^{6}=- t^{6} + 15 t^{4} - 15 t^{2} + 1,\qquad \operatorname{Im}(1+it)^{6}=6 t^{5} - 20 t^{3} + 6 t.\]

Divide the imaginary part by the real part:

\[\tan 6\theta=\frac{6 t^{5} - 20 t^{3} + 6 t}{- t^{6} + 15 t^{4} - 15 t^{2} + 1}.\]

This quotient requires \(\cos\theta\cos 6\theta\ne0\).

(b)

The numerator is \(2t(3t^4-10t^2+3)\). Set \(6\theta=k\pi\). In one tangent period, discard \(t=0\) and the undefined value at \(\theta=\pi/2\). The four remaining angles are those listed.

(c)

The two squared values solve \(3v^2-10v+3=0\), and each occurs twice among the four squared roots. Thus the square sum is \(2(10/3)=20/3\). The quartic has constant-to-leading coefficient ratio 1, so its four-root product is 1.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the sixth power of 1+it.

(b)

One candidate angle has undefined tangent; another comes from the factor t.

(c)

Count each squared value twice.

marking_criteria.description_html: Form the quotient with the correct domain.
Keep exactly the four valid nonzero tangent values.
Find the sum of squares with multiplicity.
Find the product of the four signed roots.

questions.title: A transformation with a negative exponent
questions.prompt_html:
The transformation \(T\) is defined by \(w=(\sqrt3-i)^{-4}z\).

  1. Describe \(T\) geometrically, giving an exact scale factor and rotation angle.

    [3]

  2. Find the image of \(z=8+8\sqrt3i\).

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\text{Scale factor }\frac1{16};\quad\text{rotation }\frac{2\pi}{3}\text{ anticlockwise about }O.\]

(b)

\[w=-1.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sqrt3-i=2e^{-i\pi/6},\qquad(\sqrt3-i)^{-4}=\frac1{16}e^{2\pi i/3}.\]

Multiplication by this complex number scales distances from the origin by 1/16 and adds 2π/3 to arguments.

(b)

The point is \(16e^{i\pi/3}\), so its image is \(e^{i\pi}=-1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

A negative exponent inverts the modulus and reverses the argument before multiplication.

(b)

Use modulus and argument rather than a fourth-power Cartesian expansion.

marking_criteria.description_html: Write the multiplier base in polar form.
State both geometric effects and their centre.

questions.title: Two concentric root triangles
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(z^6-7z^3-8=0\).

  1. Factor the polynomial as a product of two cubics in \(z\).

    [3]

  2. Find all six roots in exact Cartesian form.

    [5]

  3. Describe the two root triangles geometrically. Find the sum of the squares of the moduli of all six roots.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[z^6-7z^3-8=(z^3-8)(z^3+1).\]

(b)

\[2,\ -1+i\sqrt3,\ -1-i\sqrt3,\ -1,\ \frac12+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i,\ \frac12-\frac{\sqrt3}{2}i.\]

(c)

\[\text{Equilateral triangles of radii }2\text{ and }1,\text{ rotated by }\pi/3;\qquad\sum|z_j|^2=15.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(u=z^3\). The quadratic is \(u^2-7u-8=(u-8)(u+1)\), giving the displayed factorisation.

(b)

For \(z^3=8\), the roots are \(2e^{2\pi ik/3}\). For \(z^3=-1\), the roots are \(e^{i(\pi/3+2\pi k/3)}\), \(k=0,1,2\).

Converting the six standard angles gives the stated Cartesian values. The two sets have different moduli, so they do not overlap.

(c)

Each cubic contributes three equally spaced arguments, so both triangles are equilateral with centre O. The radius-1 triangle is rotated by \(\pi/3\) relative to the radius-2 triangle.

\[\sum|z_j|^2=3\cdot2^2+3\cdot1^2=15.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

First use a quadratic in z cubed.

(b)

One triangle has radius 2 and the other radius 1.

(c)

This is a sum of squared moduli, not a sum of complex squares.

marking_criteria.description_html: Explain the relative rotation and equilateral shape.

questions.title: A shifted fourth-power integral
questions.prompt_html:
A complex-number derivation is required for the identity.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cos^4u\) as a linear combination of \(1,\cos2u,\cos4u\).

    [4]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos^4(\theta+\pi/6)\,d\theta\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{4}=z^{4} + 4 z^{2} + 6 + \frac{4}{z^{2}} + \frac{1}{z^{4}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{4}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{4}\theta=\frac{\cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{2} + \frac{\cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{8} + \frac{3}{8}.\]

The identity is valid for every real angle; replace \(\theta\) by \(u\).

(b)

Put \(u=\theta+\pi/6\). Both limits move: \(u\) runs from \(\pi/6\) to \(\pi/3\).

\[\left[\frac38u+\frac14\sin2u+\frac1{32}\sin4u\right]_{\pi/6}^{\pi/3}=\frac\pi{16}-\frac{\sqrt3}{32}.\]

The sine-of-double-angle contributions cancel; the quadruple-angle contributions do not.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand \((z+z^{-1})^4\).

(b)

Shift both endpoints, not only the integrand.

questions.title: A sixth power with a triple-angle argument
questions.prompt_html:
Take \(z=e^{iu}\).

  1. Use the expansion of \((z-z^{-1})^6\) to express \(\sin^6u\) in multiple-angle form.

    [5]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/9}\sin^6(3x)\,dx\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{6}=z^{6} - 6 z^{4} + 15 z^{2} - 20 + \frac{15}{z^{2}} - \frac{6}{z^{4}} + \frac{1}{z^{6}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{6}i^{6}\). This gives

\[\sin^{6}\theta=- \frac{15 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{3 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} - \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{5}{16}.\]

Rename the angle \(u\).

(b)

With \(u=3x\), the integral becomes \(\tfrac13\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^6u\,du\).

\[=\frac13\left[\frac5{16}u-\frac{15}{64}\sin2u+\frac3{64}\sin4u-\frac1{192}\sin6u\right]_0^{\pi/3}=- \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{64} + \frac{5 \pi}{144}.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The factor \(i^6\) reverses all the signs.

(b)

Keep the one-third Jacobian factor throughout.

questions.title: Six secants and an inverse-square sum
questions.prompt_html:
Give a complete set of exact roots.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that \(\displaystyle\sec6\theta=\frac{\sec^6\theta}{32-48\sec^2\theta+18\sec^4\theta-\sec^6\theta}\), stating the required restrictions.

    [6]

  2. Hence solve \(x^{6} \left(-1 + \sqrt{2}\right) - 18 \sqrt{2} x^{4} + 48 \sqrt{2} x^{2} - 32 \sqrt{2}=0\), expressing each root as \(\sec(q\pi)\).

    [4]

  3. Evaluate \(\sum_jx_j^{-2}\), where the six roots are \(x_j\).

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{6}=\cos 6\theta+i\sin 6\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 6\theta=c^{6} - 15 c^{4} u^{2} + 15 c^{2} u^{4} - u^{6}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 6\theta=32 \cos^{6}\theta - 48 \cos^{4}\theta + 18 \cos^{2}\theta - 1.\]

Take reciprocals, then multiply numerator and denominator by \(\sec^6\theta\). Both \(\cos\theta\) and \(\cos6\theta\) must be nonzero.

(b)

The polynomial rearranges to \(x^6=-\sqrt2(32-48x^2+18x^4-x^6)\). Thus \(\sec6\theta=-\sqrt2\), or \(\cos6\theta=-1/\sqrt2\).

\[6\theta=2k\pi\pm\frac{3\pi}{4}.\]

In \([0,\pi]\), the six angles are

\[\frac{\pi}{8},\ \frac{5 \pi}{24},\ \frac{11 \pi}{24},\ \frac{13 \pi}{24},\ \frac{19 \pi}{24},\ \frac{7 \pi}{8}.\]

None has zero cosine. The six secants are distinct and exhaust the degree of the polynomial.

(c)

The reciprocal roots are six cosines. Equivalently, the reciprocal polynomial has leading coefficient \(-32\sqrt2\), zero next coefficient, and next coefficient \(48\sqrt2\). Its pairwise-product sum is \(-3/2\), so the sum of its squared roots is \(0-2(-3/2)=3\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Derive the cosine identity first.

(b)

Solve the cosine equation on an interval where cosine is injective.

(c)

Use the polynomial with reversed coefficients.

marking_criteria.description_html: Expand the real part of the sixth power.

questions.title: A tangent quartic with radical roots
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(t=\tan\theta\).

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that \(\displaystyle\cos4\theta=\frac{1-6t^2+t^4}{(1+t^2)^2}\).

    [4]

  2. Hence solve \(t^4-14t^2+1=0\), giving each root both as \(\tan(q\pi)\) and in radical form.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The real part of \((\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)^4\) is \(\cos^4\theta-6\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta+\sin^4\theta\). Divide by \(\cos^4\theta\), and use \(\sec^4\theta=(1+t^2)^2\).

\[(1+t^2)^2\cos4\theta=1-6t^2+t^4.\]

(b)

The equation is \(2(1-6t^2+t^4)=(1+t^2)^2\), hence \(\cos4\theta=1/2\). The four tangent values arise at \(\pi/12,5\pi/12,7\pi/12,11\pi/12\).

\[t^2=7\pm4\sqrt3=(2\pm\sqrt3)^2.\]

Taking both signs gives all four exact roots. Assign the signs according to the tangent quadrants.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Express cosine to the fourth in terms of tangent after taking the real part.

(b)

The positive squared roots are perfect squares of quadratic surds.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the tangent identity to obtain the denominator.

questions.title: A scaled sine equation and excluded endpoints
questions.prompt_html:
Use a complex-number argument for the multiple-angle identity.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to prove \(\sin8\theta=8\sin\theta\cos\theta(1-10\sin^2\theta+24\sin^4\theta-16\sin^6\theta)\).

    [6]

  2. Hence solve \(x^6-6x^4+10x^2-4=0\), writing roots as \(2\sin(q\pi)\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(s=\sin\theta\), \(c=\cos\theta\). The imaginary part of \((c+is)^8\) is

\[8c^7s-56c^5s^3+56c^3s^5-8cs^7=8sc(c^6-7c^4s^2+7c^2s^4-s^6).\]

Replace \(c^2\) by \(1-s^2\) inside the bracket. Expansion gives

\[(1-s^2)^3-7(1-s^2)^2s^2+7(1-s^2)s^4-s^6=1-10s^2+24s^4-16s^6.\]

(b)

For \(x=2\sin\theta\), the polynomial is \(-4(1-10\sin^2\theta+24\sin^4\theta-16\sin^6\theta)\). Choose \(-\pi/2\lt\theta\lt\pi/2\).

The equation \(\sin8\theta=0\) gives \(\theta=k\pi/8\). Discard \(\theta=0\), where the factored sine vanishes; the original polynomial at \(x=0\) is \(-4\). The endpoints would have \(x=\pm2\), also not roots. The remaining six angles are listed.

Sine is injective on the chosen interval, so six distinct roots have been obtained; they account for the degree.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor out sine times cosine before eliminating cosine squared.

(b)

Do not turn zeros of the removed sine–cosine factor into polynomial roots.

marking_criteria.description_html: Give six distinct roots and justify completeness.

questions.title: The reciprocal of a seventh sine power
questions.prompt_html:
Assume \(\sin\theta\ne0\).

  1. By expanding \((z-z^{-1})^7\), with \(z=e^{i\theta}\), express \(\csc^7\theta\) as a quotient with a constant numerator and a denominator involving \(\sin\theta,\sin3\theta,\sin5\theta,\sin7\theta\).

    [6]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{7}=z^{7} - 7 z^{5} + 21 z^{3} - 35 z + \frac{35}{z} - \frac{21}{z^{3}} + \frac{7}{z^{5}} - \frac{1}{z^{7}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{7}i^{7}\). This gives

\[\sin^{7}\theta=\frac{35 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{21 \sin{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{\sin{\left(7 \theta \right)}}{64}.\]

The denominator in the displayed answer is exactly \(64\sin^7\theta\). It is nonzero under the stated restriction, so taking the reciprocal is legitimate.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Keep track of \(i^7=-i\) before taking reciprocals.

marking_criteria.description_html: Take the reciprocal with the domain restriction.

questions.title: Seven real roots from one cosine equation
questions.prompt_html:
All polynomial roots are to be accounted for.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cos7\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\cos\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Hence solve \(128x^7-224x^5+112x^3-14x+1=0\), expressing every root as \(\cos(q\pi)\).

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{7}=\cos 7\theta+i\sin 7\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 7\theta=c^{7} - 21 c^{5} u^{2} + 35 c^{3} u^{4} - 7 c u^{6}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 7\theta=64 \cos^{7}\theta - 112 \cos^{5}\theta + 56 \cos^{3}\theta - 7 \cos\theta.\]

(b)

The equation is \(2\cos7\theta+1=0\). Thus \(7\theta=2k\pi\pm2\pi/3\). On \([0,\pi]\), the seven angles are

\[\frac{2 \pi}{21},\ \frac{4 \pi}{21},\ \frac{8 \pi}{21},\ \frac{10 \pi}{21},\ \frac{2 \pi}{3},\ \frac{16 \pi}{21},\ \frac{20 \pi}{21}.\]

Cosine is strictly decreasing on this interval; the seven values are distinct. Seven verified roots exhaust a seventh-degree polynomial.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take real parts of the seventh power and eliminate the even sine powers.

(b)

Use an injective cosine interval to prevent repeated roots.

questions.title: Cube roots after a complex translation
questions.prompt_html:
Consider \(\left(z - 1 + 2 i\right)^{3}=- 4 \sqrt{2} + 4 \sqrt{2} i\).

  1. Find all roots in the form \(z=1 - 2 i+re^{i\theta}\), where \(r\gt0\) and \(0\leq\theta\lt2\pi\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

First write the right-hand side in modulus–argument form:

\[- 4 \sqrt{2} + 4 \sqrt{2} i=8e^{i(\frac{3 \pi}{4})}.\]

All arguments are obtained before reducing to the requested interval:

\[\theta_k=\frac{\frac{3 \pi}{4}+2k\pi}{3},\quad k=0,\ldots,2.\]

Take the positive cube root of the modulus. Finally undo the translation.

\[z=1 - 2 i+2e^{i\theta},\qquad \theta=\frac{\pi}{4},\ \frac{11 \pi}{12},\ \frac{19 \pi}{12}.\]

There are 3 distinct roots, which accounts for the degree of the equation.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Separate modulus and argument; include all values obtained by adding multiples of \(2\pi\).

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the modulus and a correct argument.
Take the root of the modulus and divide each admissible argument.
Give every distinct root in the requested form and interval.

questions.title: Seven cosecant roots with a negative target
questions.prompt_html:
Keep the roots distinct when selecting the angles.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to derive an expression for \(\sin7\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\sin\theta\), and hence obtain an expression for \(\csc7\theta\) in terms of \(\csc\theta\).

    [6]

  2. Hence solve \(\sqrt{3} x^{7} + 14 x^{6} - 112 x^{4} + 224 x^{2} - 128=0\), expressing each root as \(\csc(q\pi)\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{7}=\cos 7\theta+i\sin 7\theta.\]

Expand and equate imaginary parts:

\[\sin 7\theta=7 c^{6} u - 35 c^{4} u^{3} + 21 c^{2} u^{5} - u^{7}.\]

Use \(c^2=1-u^2\).

\[\sin 7\theta=- 64 \sin^{7}\theta + 112 \sin^{5}\theta - 56 \sin^{3}\theta + 7 \sin\theta.\]

Take reciprocals and multiply by \(\csc^7\theta\). The resulting quotient requires \(\sin\theta\sin7\theta\ne0\).

(b)

With \(x=\csc\theta\), the equation says \(\sin7\theta=-\sqrt3/2\). Therefore

\[7\theta=-\frac\pi3+2k\pi\quad\text{or}\quad7\theta=\frac{4\pi}{3}+2k\pi.\]

Choose \(-\pi/2\leq\theta\leq\pi/2\), where sine is injective. The seven resulting angles are

\[- \frac{8 \pi}{21},\ - \frac{\pi}{3},\ - \frac{2 \pi}{21},\ - \frac{\pi}{21},\ \frac{4 \pi}{21},\ \frac{5 \pi}{21},\ \frac{10 \pi}{21}.\]

None has zero sine. Their reciprocals are seven distinct roots, exhausting the degree. Negative angles are permitted in the requested rational-multiple form.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The imaginary part of the seventh power produces the sine polynomial.

(b)

Choose one interval on which sine is one-to-one, and then take reciprocals.

questions.title: A scaled cosecant polynomial
questions.prompt_html:
The factor 2 in the final form is essential.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\sin5\theta\) as a polynomial in \(\sin\theta\).

    [5]

  2. Hence solve \(x^5-20x^4+320x^2-1024=0\), writing all roots as \(2\csc(q\pi)\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{5}=\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta.\]

Expand and equate imaginary parts:

\[\sin 5\theta=5 c^{4} u - 10 c^{2} u^{3} + u^{5}.\]

Use \(c^2=1-u^2\).

\[\sin 5\theta=16 \sin^{5}\theta - 20 \sin^{3}\theta + 5 \sin\theta.\]

(b)
