Put \(\sin\theta=2/x\). Multiplying the equation \(\sin5\theta=1/2\) by \(2x^5\) gives

\[20x^4-320x^2+1024=x^5.\]

Use \(5\theta=\pi/6+2k\pi\) or \(5\theta=5\pi/6+2k\pi\), and choose \(-\pi/2\leq\theta\leq\pi/2\). This gives

\[- \frac{11 \pi}{30},\ - \frac{7 \pi}{30},\ \frac{\pi}{30},\ \frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{13 \pi}{30}.\]

All five sine values are nonzero and distinct. The five verified roots exhaust the polynomial degree, so the substitution has not omitted any further roots.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take imaginary parts, then replace cosine squared.

(b)

Use sine equal to 2/x, not x or 1/x.

questions.title: Harmonic cancellation and a hidden factorisation
questions.prompt_html:
The last part asks for real roots only.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to derive multiple-angle forms for \(\cos^8\theta\) and \(\sin^8\theta\), and hence show that their sum is \((35+28\cos4\theta+\cos8\theta)/64\).

    [6]

  2. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/3}(\cos^8(x/2)+\sin^8(x/2))\,dx\).

    [4]

  3. Find every real root of \(32c^8+32(1-c^2)^4-17=0\), and justify why there are no additional real roots.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{8}=z^{8} + 8 z^{6} + 28 z^{4} + 56 z^{2} + 70 + \frac{56}{z^{2}} + \frac{28}{z^{4}} + \frac{8}{z^{6}} + \frac{1}{z^{8}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{8}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{8}\theta=\frac{7 \cos{\left(2 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{7 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{32} + \frac{\cos{\left(6 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{128} + \frac{35}{128}.\]

Apply the complementary-angle substitution to obtain the sine expression. Terms in \(\cos2\theta\) and \(\cos6\theta\) change sign, so those terms cancel on addition.

\[\frac{7 \cos{\left(4 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\cos{\left(8 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{35}{64}\]

(b)

Put \(\theta=x/2\) into the identity, so the frequencies become 2 and 4 in x.

\[\left[\frac{35x}{64}+\frac7{32}\sin2x+\frac1{256}\sin4x\right]_0^{\pi/3}=\frac{35\pi}{192}+\frac{55\sqrt3}{512}.\]

(c)

Let \(v=8c^4-8c^2+1\). Direct expansion, or the identity in (a), gives

\[32c^8+32(1-c^2)^4-17=v(v+14).\]

For every real \(c\), \(v=8(c^2-1/2)^2-1\geq-1\), so \(v+14\gt0\). Only \(v=0\) is possible. This is \(\cos4\theta=0\) with \(c=\cos\theta\); the four displayed values are distinct and solve the quartic. The positivity argument rules out the other factor for all real c, including values outside [-1,1].
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The complementary-angle substitution saves a second full expansion.

(b)

Substitution into the harmonic identity already changes the frequencies.

(c)

A substitution c=cos(theta) alone would not exclude real roots outside [-1,1].

marking_criteria.description_html: Expand the cosine power using complex numbers.
Prove the second factor is always positive for real c.
Find all four roots of the remaining quartic.

questions.title: A ratio of seventh-power harmonics
questions.prompt_html:
Assume \(\cos\theta\ne0\).

  1. Use \((z+z^{-1})^7\) and \((z-z^{-1})^7\), where \(z=e^{i\theta}\), to express \(\tan^7\theta\) as a quotient of two linear combinations of multiple-angle sines and cosines.

    [7]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{7}=z^{7} - 7 z^{5} + 21 z^{3} - 35 z + \frac{35}{z} - \frac{21}{z^{3}} + \frac{7}{z^{5}} - \frac{1}{z^{7}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{7}i^{7}\). This gives

\[\sin^{7}\theta=\frac{35 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{21 \sin{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{7 \sin{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{64} - \frac{\sin{\left(7 \theta \right)}}{64}.\]

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z+z^{-1})^{7}=z^{7} + 7 z^{5} + 21 z^{3} + 35 z + \frac{35}{z} + \frac{21}{z^{3}} + \frac{7}{z^{5}} + \frac{1}{z^{7}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{7}i^{0}\). This gives

\[\cos^{7}\theta=\frac{35 \cos{\left(\theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{21 \cos{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{7 \cos{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{64} + \frac{\cos{\left(7 \theta \right)}}{64}.\]

Take the quotient. The denominator equals \(64\cos^7\theta\) and is nonzero exactly when the original tangent is defined.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

An odd power of i affects the sine expansion before the quotient is formed.

questions.title: A sine-power identity with rescaled integration
questions.prompt_html:
Derive the identity rather than quoting a standard power-reduction formula.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(16\sin^5u\) in the form \(A\sin u+B\sin3u+C\sin5u\).

    [5]

  2. Hence evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}32\sin^5(2\theta)\,d\theta\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Let \(z=e^{i\theta}\), so \(z+z^{-1}=2\cos\theta\) and \(z-z^{-1}=2i\sin\theta\).

\[(z-z^{-1})^{5}=z^{5} - 5 z^{3} + 10 z - \frac{10}{z} + \frac{5}{z^{3}} - \frac{1}{z^{5}}.\]

Pair terms with opposite exponents, using \(z^j+z^{-j}=2\cos j\theta\) and \(z^j-z^{-j}=2i\sin j\theta\), and divide by \(2^{5}i^{5}\). This gives

\[\sin^{5}\theta=\frac{5 \sin{\left(\theta \right)}}{8} - \frac{5 \sin{\left(3 \theta \right)}}{16} + \frac{\sin{\left(5 \theta \right)}}{16}.\]

Multiply by 16 and rename the angle u. Thus \(A=10,B=-5,C=1\).

(b)

Put \(u=2\theta\). Then the integral is \(16\int_0^{\pi/3}\sin^5u\,du\).

\[\left[-10\cos u+\frac53\cos3u-\frac15\cos5u\right]_0^{\pi/3}=\frac{53}{30}.\]

The nonzero value of the antiderivative at the lower endpoint must be subtracted.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Expand the fifth power of \(z-z^{-1}\).

(b)

Keep the lower endpoint when integrating odd sines.

questions.title: Sine roots, a product and a reciprocal sum
questions.prompt_html:
All requested final quantities should be exact.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to prove \(\sin7\theta=7\sin\theta-56\sin^3\theta+112\sin^5\theta-64\sin^7\theta\).

    [6]

  2. Show that \(\sin^2(\pi/7),\sin^2(2\pi/7),\sin^2(3\pi/7)\) are exactly the three roots of \(64u^3-112u^2+56u-7=0\).

    [4]

  3. Deduce \(\prod_{k=1}^6\sin(k\pi/7)\) and \(\sum_{k=1}^3\csc^2(k\pi/7)\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sin7\theta=7\sin\theta-56\sin^3\theta+112\sin^5\theta-64\sin^7\theta.\]

(b)

The three stated squared sine values are all the roots.

(c)

\[\prod_{k=1}^6\sin\frac{k\pi}{7}=\frac7{64},\qquad\sum_{k=1}^3\csc^2\frac{k\pi}{7}=8.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{7}=\cos 7\theta+i\sin 7\theta.\]

Expand and equate imaginary parts:

\[\sin 7\theta=7 c^{6} u - 35 c^{4} u^{3} + 21 c^{2} u^{5} - u^{7}.\]

Use \(c^2=1-u^2\).

\[\sin 7\theta=- 64 \sin^{7}\theta + 112 \sin^{5}\theta - 56 \sin^{3}\theta + 7 \sin\theta.\]

(b)

At \(\theta=k\pi/7\), the left side of (a) is zero. For \(k=1,2,3\), sine is positive and nonzero, so division by it gives the cubic in \(u=\sin^2\theta\). These three angles lie strictly between 0 and \(\pi/2\), where sine is increasing. The three squared values are distinct and exhaust a cubic.

(c)

Pair \(\sin(k\pi/7)\) with \(\sin((7-k)\pi/7)\). The six-sine product is the product of the three u-roots, equal to \(7/64\).

The sum of pairwise products of the u-roots is \(56/64\). Since their product is \(7/64\),

\[\sum\frac1u=\frac{56/64}{7/64}=8.\]
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take imaginary parts and factor one sine before simplification.

(b)

Verify nonzero sine before division and distinctness after squaring.

(c)

The six-factor sine product already contains each positive sine twice.

marking_criteria.description_html: Divide by a nonzero sine and substitute u.

questions.title: Selecting the correct quadratic surd
questions.prompt_html:
Do not use numerical trigonometric values.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to derive \(\cos5\theta=\cos\theta(16\cos^4\theta-20\cos^2\theta+5)\).

    [5]

  2. Hence find the exact values of \(\cos(\pi/10)\) and \(\cos(3\pi/10)\), justifying the choice of signs.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{5}=\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 5\theta=c^{5} - 10 c^{3} u^{2} + 5 c u^{4}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 5\theta=16 \cos^{5}\theta - 20 \cos^{3}\theta + 5 \cos\theta.\]

Factor one cosine from the polynomial.

(b)

For both angles, \(\cos5\theta=0\) but \(\cos\theta\ne0\). Therefore \(u=\cos^2\theta\) satisfies

\[16u^2-20u+5=0,\qquad u=\frac{5\pm\sqrt5}{8}.\]

Both cosines are positive. Cosine is decreasing on \((0,\pi/2)\), so the smaller angle \(\pi/10\) has the larger square. Take positive square roots with that ordering.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take real parts of the fifth power.

(b)

Both the sign of the cosine and the order of the two squares need justification.

marking_criteria.description_html: Assign the larger root to the smaller angle.

questions.title: Three cosine squares from a sixth-angle identity
questions.prompt_html:
A product of three squares can be found without finding each square separately.

  1. Use de Moivre’s theorem to prove \(\cos6\theta=32\cos^6\theta-48\cos^4\theta+18\cos^2\theta-1\).

    [5]

  2. Hence find the exact sum and product of \(\cos^2(\pi/12),\cos^2(\pi/4),\cos^2(5\pi/12)\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{6}=\cos 6\theta+i\sin 6\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 6\theta=c^{6} - 15 c^{4} u^{2} + 15 c^{2} u^{4} - u^{6}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 6\theta=32 \cos^{6}\theta - 48 \cos^{4}\theta + 18 \cos^{2}\theta - 1.\]

(b)

The three angles give \(\cos6\theta=0\). Their cosine squares are distinct and satisfy

\[32u^3-48u^2+18u-1=0.\]

They therefore exhaust the three roots. By the coefficient relations, their sum is \(48/32=3/2\) and their product is \(1/32\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Eliminate sine using only even powers.

(b)

Find the polynomial for the squares, then use its coefficients.

marking_criteria.description_html: Obtain the cubic in the squared cosine.

questions.title: Eighteenth roots with a missing subset
questions.prompt_html:
Do not retain roots introduced by multiplication.

  1. Write down the six sixth roots of unity.

    [2]

  2. Find all roots of \(z^{12}+z^6+1=0\), in the form \(e^{i\theta}\), with \(0\leq\theta\lt2\pi\).

    [4]

  3. State how many of these roots are real.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Every root has modulus 1, and its argument is a multiple of \(2\pi/6\).

(b)

\[(z^6-1)(z^{12}+z^6+1)=z^{18}-1.\]

Take all eighteenth roots, then exclude the sixth roots. Among \(e^{ik\pi/9}\), the sixth roots occur exactly when k is a multiple of 3. The twelve retained roots are distinct and exhaust the degree.

(c)

The only real points on the unit circle are \(1\) and \(-1\). Both are sixth roots and were excluded.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use six equally spaced arguments.

(b)

The excluded set is identified by divisibility of the argument index.

(c)

Check the two real points of the unit circle.

questions.title: Two factors and no overlapping roots
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(P(z)=z^7-(1+i)z^4-4z^3+4(1+i)\).

  1. Find complex constants \(a,b\) such that \(P(z)=(z^4-a)(z^3-b)\).

    [2]

  2. Hence find every root in exponential form with angles in \([0,2\pi)\). Explain why there are seven distinct roots.

    [5]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[a=4,\qquad b=1+i.\]

(b)

\[z=\sqrt2e^{ik\pi/2},\ k=0,1,2,3;\qquad z=2^{1/6}e^{i(\pi/12+2k\pi/3)},\ k=0,1,2.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Expansion gives \(z^7-bz^4-az^3+ab\). Compare the coefficients of \(z^4\) and \(z^3\); the constant term then also agrees.

(b)

The first factor gives \(z^4=4\): radius \(4^{1/4}=\sqrt2\), with four arguments separated by \(\pi/2\). The second gives \(z^3=1+i=\sqrt2e^{i\pi/4}\): radius \(2^{1/6}\), with arguments \(\pi/12,3\pi/4,17\pi/12\).

The families have different moduli, \(\sqrt2\ne2^{1/6}\), so no root occurs in both. All seven are distinct.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Compare the two middle coefficients first.

(b)

Check possible overlap by comparing moduli before comparing arguments.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find a and b and check the constant.
Find the four roots from the first factor.
Find the three roots from the second factor.

questions.title: A translated regular hexagon
questions.prompt_html:
A complex number \(w\) satisfies \((w-2i)^6=64\).

  1. Find all possible values of \(w\), giving exact Cartesian answers.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Put \(v=w-2i\). Then \(v=2e^{ik\pi/3}\), \(k=0,\ldots,5\), since \(64^{1/6}=2\). Convert the six standard angles into Cartesian components, then add \(2i\) to each. These are six vertices of a regular hexagon of radius 2 centred at the point representing \(2i\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Take roots before undoing the translation.

marking_criteria.description_html: Introduce the shifted variable and find radius 2.

questions.title: A ninth-degree polynomial with five real roots
questions.prompt_html:
Use factorisation to separate the real and non-real branches.

  1. Find the four roots of \(w^4=-1\) in exponential form. State whether any is real.

    [2]

  2. Use de Moivre’s theorem to express \(\cos5\theta\) in terms of \(\cos\theta\).

    [4]

  3. Hence find all real roots of \(16x^9-20x^7+21x^5-20x^3+5x=0\), in cosine form.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[w=e^{i(\pi/4+k\pi/2)},\quad k=0,1,2,3;\quad\text{none is real}.\]

(b)

\[\cos5\theta=16\cos^5\theta-20\cos^3\theta+5\cos\theta.\]

(c)

\[x=\cos\frac\pi{10},\ \cos\frac{3\pi}{10},\ \cos\frac\pi2,\ \cos\frac{7\pi}{10},\ \cos\frac{9\pi}{10}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Write \(-1=e^{i\pi}\). The root angles are \(\pi/4,3\pi/4,5\pi/4,7\pi/4\), none of which lies on the real axis.

(b)

Put \(c=\cos\theta\) and \(u=\sin\theta\). De Moivre gives

\[(c+iu)^{5}=\cos 5\theta+i\sin 5\theta.\]

Expand and equate real parts:

\[\cos 5\theta=c^{5} - 10 c^{3} u^{2} + 5 c u^{4}.\]

Use \(u^2=1-c^2\).

\[\cos 5\theta=16 \cos^{5}\theta - 20 \cos^{3}\theta + 5 \cos\theta.\]

(c)

\[16x^9-20x^7+21x^5-20x^3+5x=(x^4+1)(16x^5-20x^3+5x).\]

For real \(x\), \(x^4+1\gt0\). The second factor is zero at \(x=\cos\theta\) when \(5\theta=\pi/2+k\pi\). The five displayed angles lie in \([0,\pi]\), give distinct values and exhaust the degree of the second factor. They include the zero root \(\cos(\pi/2)=0\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use the argument pi rather than zero.

(b)

Use the real part of the fifth power.

(c)

Do not discard the zero root of the fifth-degree factor.

marking_criteria.description_html: Exclude the first factor for real x.
Give all five distinct real roots, including zero.

questions.title: A rotated pentagon and its nearest vertex
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(w\) be any root of \(z^5=16+16\sqrt3i\).

  1. Write down the fifth roots of unity.

    [1]

  2. Find the five roots of the given equation in exponential form and sketch them on an Argand diagram.

    [4]

  3. Express \(\displaystyle\sum_{j=0}^4(w/2)^j\) as a quotient in terms of \(w\).

    [3]

  4. Identify the root nearest to the point representing 3, and give the exact minimum distance.

    [3]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[e^{2k\pi i/5},\quad k=0,1,2,3,4.\]

(b)

\[z_k=2e^{i(\pi/15+2k\pi/5)},\quad k=0,1,2,3,4.\]

(c)

\[\frac{1-i\sqrt3}{2-w}.\]

(d)

\[z=2e^{i\pi/15},\qquad d_{\min}=\sqrt{13-12\cos(\pi/15)}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

They have unit modulus and arguments separated by \(2\pi/5\).

(b)

\[16+16\sqrt3i=32e^{i\pi/3}.\]

Take fifth roots: the radius is 2 and the initial angle is \(\pi/15\). Multiplication by the fifth roots of unity generates the other four roots. The sketch is a regular pentagon centred at the origin, rotated by \(\pi/15\).

(c)

Since \((w/2)^5=(1+i\sqrt3)/2\ne1\), in particular \(w\ne2\). Apply the geometric formula:

\[\sum_{j=0}^4(w/2)^j=\frac{1-(w/2)^5}{1-w/2}=\frac{(1-i\sqrt3)/2}{(2-w)/2}=\frac{1-i\sqrt3}{2-w}.\]

(d)

\[|2e^{i\theta}-3|^2=4+9-12\cos\theta.\]

The five arguments, reduced about zero if necessary, have smallest absolute value at \(\theta=\pi/15\). This root has the largest real part and hence the least distance. Substitute that angle into the distance formula.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use a complete turn divided into five equal angles.

(b)

Rotate the fifth roots of unity, then scale by 2.

(c)

Use the known fifth power of w/2.

(d)

For fixed radius, nearest to a positive real point means largest cosine.

marking_criteria.description_html: Find the polar form of the right side.
Use the geometric sum with the correct starting term.
Express the squared distance in terms of cosine.

questions.title: A cosine sum and rigorous rectangle bounds
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer. Divide \([0,\pi/6]\) into \(n\) equal intervals, and consider \(f(x)=\cos2x\). Rectangles use either the left endpoint or the right endpoint of each interval.

  1. By summing powers of \(e^{i\delta}\), prove that, when \(\sin(\delta/2)\ne0\), \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\cos(r\delta)=\frac{\sin(n\delta/2)\cos((n-1)\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}\).

    [3]

  2. Show that a strict upper bound for \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos2x\,dx\) is \(\displaystyle U_n=\frac{\pi}{12n}\frac{\cos(\pi/6-\pi/(6n))}{\sin(\pi/(6n))}\).

    [4]

  3. Obtain a strict lower bound \(L_n\) and simplify \(U_n-L_n\).

    [4]

  4. Find the common limit of \(U_n\) and \(L_n\), and the least integer \(n\) for which \(U_n-L_n\lt\pi/12000\).

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\cos(r\delta)=\frac{\sin(n\delta/2)\cos((n-1)\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}.\]

(b)

\[\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos2x\,dx\lt U_n=\frac{\pi}{12n}\frac{\cos(\pi/6-\pi/(6n))}{\sin(\pi/(6n))}.\]

(c)

\[L_n=U_n-\frac{\pi}{12n},\qquad U_n-L_n=\frac{\pi}{12n}.\]

(d)

\[\lim U_n=\lim L_n=\frac{\sqrt3}{4},\qquad n_{\min}=1001.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}e^{ir\delta}=\frac{1-e^{in\delta}}{1-e^{i\delta}}=e^{i(n-1)\delta/2}\frac{\sin(n\delta/2)}{\sin(\delta/2)}.\]

To obtain the second equality, factor \(-2i e^{in\delta/2}\) from the numerator and \(-2i e^{i\delta/2}\) from the denominator. The remaining sine quotient is real. Equating real parts proves the formula.

(b)

The width is \(h=\pi/(6n)\). The function is strictly decreasing on the interval, so the left-endpoint rectangles lie above it except at their left edges.

\[U_n=\frac{\pi}{6n}\sum_{r=0}^{n-1}\cos\frac{r\pi}{3n}.\]

Apply (a) with \(\delta=\pi/(3n)\). Since \(\sin(n\delta/2)=\sin(\pi/6)=1/2\), the required expression follows. Each interval has positive width and contributes a strict excess.

(c)

Right endpoints give

\[L_n=\frac{\pi}{6n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\cos\frac{r\pi}{3n}\lt\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos2x\,dx.\]

The two sums share all interior endpoint terms. Thus

\[U_n-L_n=\frac{\pi}{6n}\left(1-\cos\frac\pi3\right)=\frac{\pi}{12n}.\]

Subtract this gap from the expression in (b) to obtain the stated lower bound.

(d)

\[\int_0^{\pi/6}\cos2x\,dx=\left[\frac12\sin2x\right]_0^{\pi/6}=\frac{\sqrt3}{4}.\]

The integral is between the bounds, whose gap tends to zero; hence both bounds tend to the integral.

\[\frac{\pi}{12n}\lt\frac{\pi}{12000}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n\gt1000.\]

The value 1000 gives equality, not the required strict inequality. The least admissible integer is therefore 1001.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Factor each difference of exponentials about its half-angle.

(b)

Use left endpoints and the width, not just the sum of heights.

(c)

Cancel the interior terms of the two rectangle sums.

(d)

Treat the strict inequality at the integer boundary carefully.

marking_criteria.description_html: Justify that it is a strict lower bound.
Give the lower bound and exact gap.
Justify the common limit using the gap.

questions.title: Weighted sums with a non-unit complex ratio
questions.prompt_html:
Throughout parts (b) and (c), assume \(\sin\theta\cos\theta\ne0\).

  1. Find \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}w^k\) for \(w\ne1\), where \(n\) is a positive integer.

    [2]

  2. Use de Moivre’s theorem to show that \((1+i\tan\theta)^k=\sec^k\theta(\cos k\theta+i\sin k\theta)\) for every non-negative integer \(k\).

    [3]

  3. Hence obtain formulae for \(\displaystyle C_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sec^k\theta\cos k\theta\) and \(\displaystyle S_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\sec^k\theta\sin k\theta\).

    [3]

  4. For a non-negative integer \(m\), evaluate \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{8m+1}(\sqrt2)^k\cos(k\pi/4)\) and \(\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{8m+1}(\sqrt2)^k\sin(k\pi/4)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}w^k=\frac{1-w^n}{1-w}.\]

(b)

\[(1+i\tan\theta)^k=\sec^k\theta(\cos k\theta+i\sin k\theta).\]

(c)

\[C_n=\cot\theta\sec^n\theta\sin n\theta,\qquad S_n=\cot\theta(1-\sec^n\theta\cos n\theta).\]

(d)

\[2^{4m+1}\quad\text{and}\quad1,\quad\text{respectively}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

If \(S=1+w+\cdots+w^{n-1}\), subtract \(wS\) from \(S\). The interior terms cancel, giving \((1-w)S=1-w^n\). Divide by \(1-w\ne0\).

(b)

\[1+i\tan\theta=\frac{\cos\theta+i\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}.\]

Raise both sides to the integer power \(k\) and apply de Moivre to the numerator. For \(k=0\), both sides equal 1. The factor \(\sec\theta\) need not be positive: this is an algebraic identity, not a claim that it is the positive modulus.

(c)

Set \(w=1+i\tan\theta\). It is not 1 because \(\sin\theta\ne0\). By (a) and (b),

\[C_n+iS_n=\frac{1-\sec^n\theta(\cos n\theta+i\sin n\theta)}{-i\tan\theta}.\]

Multiply the numerator by \(i\cot\theta\). Its real part is \(\cot\theta\sec^n\theta\sin n\theta\), and its imaginary part is the stated expression for \(S_n\).

(d)

Take \(n=8m+2\) and \(\theta=\pi/4\). Then \(\cot\theta=1\), \(\sec^n\theta=2^{4m+1}\), \(\sin n\theta=1\) and \(\cos n\theta=0\). Substitute in both formulae.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Subtract the sum multiplied by w.

(b)

Factor out 1/cos(theta), without assuming its sign.

(c)

Remember that 1/(-i) equals i.

(d)

Count terms before substituting the periodic angle.

marking_criteria.description_html: Rewrite the base using sine and cosine.
Apply de Moivre to its kth power.
Substitute the complex ratio into the geometric sum.
Identify both real and imaginary parts correctly.

questions.title: Finite cancellation and two infinite sums
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer.

  1. If \(w^n=1\) and \(w\ne1\), prove that \(1+w+\cdots+w^{n-1}=0\).

    [2]

  2. By considering powers of \(z=\tfrac25e^{i\theta}\), find closed forms for \(\displaystyle C=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(2/5)^r\cos r\theta\) and \(\displaystyle S=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(2/5)^r\sin r\theta\). Justify convergence.

    [6]

  3. Evaluate both sums when \(\theta=\pi/3\).

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The sum is \((1-w^n)/(1-w)\). Its numerator is zero and its denominator is not, so the sum is zero. The restriction \(w\ne1\) is essential: when \(w=1\), the sum is \(n\).

(b)

Since \(|z|=2/5\lt1\), the complex geometric series converges absolutely. Both real and imaginary series also converge absolutely by comparison with \(\sum(2/5)^r\).

\[C+iS=\frac{z}{1-z}=\frac{z(1-\overline z)}{|1-z|^2}=\frac{(2/5)(\cos\theta+i\sin\theta)-4/25}{29/25-(4/5)\cos\theta}.\]

Multiply numerator and denominator by 25 and equate real and imaginary parts. The denominator is at least \(29-20=9\), so the formulae are valid for every real \(\theta\).

(c)

Substitute \(\cos(\pi/3)=1/2\) and \(\sin(\pi/3)=\sqrt3/2\). The common denominator is 19, and the two numerators are 1 and \(5\sqrt3\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Apply the geometric formula only after checking the denominator.

(b)

The series starts at r=1, so its numerator is z, not 1.

(c)

Substitute exact trigonometric values.

marking_criteria.description_html: Use the root condition and excluded value correctly.
Give the sine formula and a valid denominator.

questions.title: A symmetric sum with exceptional angles
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer.

  1. For \(z e0\) and \(z^3 e1\), express \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=-n}^{n}z^{3r}\) as a single quotient.

    [2]

  2. Use \(z=e^{i heta}\) to show that \(\displaystyle1+2\sum_{r=1}^{n}\cos(3r heta)= rac{\sin((3n+3/2) heta)}{\sin(3 heta/2)}\), whenever \(\sin(3 heta/2) e0\).

    [4]

  3. Find the value of the finite sum on the left when \( heta=2m\pi/3\), where \(m\) is an integer.

    [1]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The first term is \(z^{-3n}\), the ratio is \(z^3\), and there are \(2n+1\) terms. Apply the finite geometric formula with these three quantities.

(b)

In the sum on the left of (a), terms with indices \(r\) and \(-r\) add to \(2\cos(3r\theta)\), with a central term 1.

\[e^{-3ni\theta}\frac{-2i e^{3(2n+1)i\theta/2}\sin(3(2n+1)\theta/2)}{-2i e^{3i\theta/2}\sin(3\theta/2)}=\frac{\sin((3n+3/2)\theta)}{\sin(3\theta/2)}.\]

The exponential factors cancel exactly. This also confirms that the sum is real.

(c)

Every cosine is \(\cos(2rm\pi)=1\). Evaluate the original finite sum rather than its undefined quotient.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

There are 2n+1 terms, not 2n.

(b)

Pair the negative and positive powers before simplifying the quotient.

(c)

Return to the finite sum, not the 0/0 formula.

marking_criteria.description_html: Identify the starting term and number of terms.
Rewrite the numerator using a half-angle sine.
Obtain the stated identity with its restriction.

questions.title: A phase-shifted sum over odd multiples
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\geq1\), and let \(\theta,\phi\) be real. Assume \(\sin\theta\ne0\) in parts (a) and (b).

  1. Sum \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{i((2r-1)\theta+\phi)}\), writing the result as a real sine quotient multiplied by one exponential.

    [3]

  2. Hence find \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\cos((2r-1)\theta+\phi)\). Also state its value at \(\theta=m\pi\), where \(m\) is an integer.

    [3]

  3. Evaluate \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\cos\!\left(\frac{(2r-1)\pi}{2n}+\frac\pi3\right)\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{i((2r-1)\theta+\phi)}=e^{i(n\theta+\phi)}\frac{\sin n\theta}{\sin\theta}.\]

(b)

\[\frac{\sin n\theta\cos(n\theta+\phi)}{\sin\theta};\qquad n(-1)^m\cos\phi\text{ when }\theta=m\pi.\]

(c)

\[-\frac{\sqrt3}{2\sin(\pi/(2n))}.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{i((2r-1)\theta+\phi)}=e^{i(\theta+\phi)}\frac{1-e^{2ni\theta}}{1-e^{2i\theta}}.\]

Use \(1-e^{2ni\theta}=-2ie^{ni\theta}\sin n\theta\) and the corresponding identity in the denominator. The remaining exponential is \(e^{i(n\theta+\phi)}\).

(b)

Take real parts in (a); the sine quotient is real. At the excluded angles, every term of the original sum is \(\cos((2r-1)m\pi+\phi)=(-1)^m\cos\phi\). There are \(n\) such terms.

(c)

Take \(\theta=\pi/(2n)\) and \(\phi=\pi/3\). Then \(\sin n\theta=1\) and \(\cos(n\theta+\phi)=\cos(5\pi/6)=-\sqrt3/2\). The denominator is nonzero for every \(n\geq1\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The first phase is theta+phi and the step is 2theta.

(b)

The exceptional angle can be evaluated term by term.

(c)

Use ntheta=pi/2 before evaluating the shifted cosine.

marking_criteria.description_html: Determine one term at an exceptional angle.

questions.title: Differentiating an even-multiple sine sum
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\geq2\) be an integer.

  1. By considering \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}z^{2r}\), where \(z=e^{i\theta}\), prove that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\sin2r\theta=\frac{\sin n\theta\sin((n+1)\theta)}{\sin\theta}\), for \(\sin\theta\ne0\).

    [6]

  2. Hence show that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}2r\cos(r\pi/n)=-n-\operatorname{cosec}^{2}(\pi/(2n))\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}z^{2r}=z^2\frac{1-z^{2n}}{1-z^2}.\]

Substitute \(z=e^{i\theta}\) and factor numerator and denominator about their half angles:

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{2ri\theta}=e^{i(n+1)\theta}\frac{\sin n\theta}{\sin\theta}.\]

The sine quotient is real, so the imaginary part gives the required sum. Division is valid precisely under the stated restriction.

(b)

This is a finite sum, so differentiate term by term. Put \(\alpha=\pi/(2n)\) only after differentiating. For \(A(\theta)=\sin n\theta\sin((n+1)\theta)\),

\[A(\alpha)=\cos\alpha,\qquad A\prime(\alpha)=-(n+1)\sin\alpha.\]

The quotient rule therefore gives

\[\left.\frac d{d\theta}\frac{A(\theta)}{\sin\theta}\right|_{\theta=\alpha}=-(n+1)-\cot^2\alpha=-n-\operatorname{cosec}^2\alpha.\]

The differentiated left side is \(\sum 2r\cos(2r\alpha)=\sum 2r\cos(r\pi/n)\), as required.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

The phase after cancellation is (n+1)theta, not ntheta.

(b)

Keep n constant during differentiation; substitute the angle at the end.

marking_criteria.description_html: Differentiate the quotient and evaluate its numerator terms.

questions.title: A weighted sine sum at roots-of-unity angles
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\geq2\) be an integer.

  1. Use a complex geometric series to prove \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}\cos2r\theta=\frac{\sin n\theta\cos((n+1)\theta)}{\sin\theta}\), for \(\sin\theta\ne0\).

    [5]

  2. Deduce that \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=1}^{n}2r\sin\frac{2r\pi}{n+1}=-(n+1)\cot\frac\pi{n+1}\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{2ri\theta}=e^{2i\theta}\frac{1-e^{2ni\theta}}{1-e^{2i\theta}}=e^{i(n+1)\theta}\frac{\sin n\theta}{\sin\theta}.\]

Take real parts. The quotient is real and defined under the stated restriction, so this yields the identity.

(b)

Differentiate the finite identity in (a). Let \(\alpha=\pi/(n+1)\) and \(B(\theta)=\sin n\theta\cos((n+1)\theta)\). Then

\[B(\alpha)=-\sin\alpha,\qquad B\prime(\alpha)=n\cos\alpha.\]

The quotient derivative at \(\alpha\) is

\[\frac{n\cos\alpha\sin\alpha+\sin\alpha\cos\alpha}{\sin^2\alpha}=(n+1)\cot\alpha.\]

The derivative of the left side is \(-\sum2r\sin2r\theta\). Move the minus sign to obtain the required result.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Use both the first term and the common ratio in the geometric series.

(b)

The derivative of a cosine contributes a minus sign.

marking_criteria.description_html: Differentiate the finite sum with its sign.
Apply the quotient rule and evaluate the two numerator terms.
Account for the minus sign in the required sum.

questions.title: A binomial sum with weights
questions.prompt_html:
Let \(n\geq1\) be an integer and \(0\lt\theta\lt\pi\).

  1. Prove that \(r\binom nr=n\binom{n-1}{r-1}\) for \(1\leq r\leq n\).

    [2]

  2. By considering \(\displaystyle\sum_{r=0}^{n}r\binom nr z^r\), with \(z=e^{i\theta}\), find closed forms for the corresponding cosine and sine sums.

    [5]

  3. Evaluate both sums in (b) when \(n=5\) and \(\theta=\pi/3\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\[r\binom nr=n\binom{n-1}{r-1}.\]

(b)

\[\begin{aligned}\sum_{r=0}^{n}r\binom nr\cos r\theta&=n2^{n-1}\cos^{n-1}(\theta/2)\cos((n+1)\theta/2),\\\sum_{r=0}^{n}r\binom nr\sin r\theta&=n2^{n-1}\cos^{n-1}(\theta/2)\sin((n+1)\theta/2).\end{aligned}\]

(c)

\[\text{Cosine sum}=-45,\qquad\text{sine sum}=0.\]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[r\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}=\frac{n!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}=n\frac{(n-1)!}{(r-1)!(n-r)!}.\]

The factorials are defined under the given index restriction.

(b)

The term for \(r=0\) vanishes. Apply (a), then put \(j=r-1\):

\[\sum_{r=1}^{n}r\binom nr z^r=nz\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{n-1}{j}z^j=nz(1+z)^{n-1}.\]

Use \(1+e^{i\theta}=2\cos(\theta/2)e^{i\theta/2}\). De Moivre gives

\[nz(1+z)^{n-1}=n2^{n-1}\cos^{n-1}(\theta/2)e^{i(n+1)\theta/2}.\]

Equate real and imaginary parts to obtain the two formulae.

(c)

The amplitude is \(5\cdot2^4(\sqrt3/2)^4=45\). The phase is \((5+1)\pi/6=\pi\), so its cosine is \(-1\) and its sine is 0.
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Cancel r from r factorial.

(b)

Shift the index after using the identity in part (a).

(c)

Calculate the amplitude and phase separately.

marking_criteria.description_html: Shift the index and use the binomial theorem.
Use de Moivre and combine the phase.
